body_text:
### Description

`HttpRemoteTaskRunner.shutdown(taskId, reason)` does not handle either `PENDING` or `PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN`. This is a per-task cancellation call, not shutdown of the runner itself: the assignment loop remains active and can launch the cancelled task.

There are two cases worth tracking separately:

1. **Cancellation while strictly `PENDING`: confirmed by CI logs.** A task remains eligible for selection even after its status is persisted as `FAILED` and HRTR receives its shutdown request.
2. **Cancellation while `PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN`: confirmed missing handling in source; the specific concurrent interleaving has not been reproduced independently.** Worker selection has already happened, and an assignment request may be about to start or already be in flight. A fix that only removes a pending ID cannot stop the assignment thread's captured work item.

### Source and CI examined

- CI run: https://github.com/FrankChen021/druid/actions/runs/34215796434
- PR whose CI exposed the behavior: https://github.com/FrankChen021/druid/pull/196 (test workload changes, not an HRTR fix)
- CI head: `ef8090de9586daffc08c851528c092982e782384`
- Matching artifact: `unit-test-reports-jdk25-55e4156d`, artifact ID `10052676864`: https://github.com/FrankChen021/druid/actions/runs/34215796434/artifacts/10052676864
- Report: `TEST-org.apache.druid.testing.embedded.indexing.autoscaler.CostBasedAutoScalerIntegrationTest.xml`
- Local source inspected: `33f7f778dfc2d8b06ca7c1d7a93f54f162526cee`. Its HRTR and TaskQueue files have no diff against the CI head.

The affected source is verified at these commits; an earliest affected release has not been established.

### Case 1: cancelled PENDING tasks are later assigned

Surefire reports **98.596 seconds** for `CostBasedAutoScalerIntegrationTest#test_autoScaler_computesOptimalTaskCountAndProducesScaleUp`.

The preceding test left tasks for `datasource_alifbaan`. One exact task ID is `index_kafka_datasource_alifbaan_7fd4f836c343694_ibbcnlhl`. The artifact contains:

```text
10:54:07.260 HRTR: Adding pending task[index_kafka_datasource_alifbaan_7fd4f836c343694_ibbcnlhl].
10:54:09.200 MetadataTaskStorage: Updating status ... status=FAILED ... errorMsg=Killing task for graceful shutdown
10:54:09.201 HRTR: Shutdown [index_kafka_datasource_alifbaan_7fd4f836c343694_ibbcnlhl] because: [Killing task for graceful shutdown]
10:54:09.354 HRTR: Assigning task [index_kafka_datasource_alifbaan_7fd4f836c343694_ibbcnlhl] to worker [10.1.1.207:8091]
10:54:09.359 HRTR: Task[index_kafka_datasource_alifbaan_7fd4f836c343694_ibbcnlhl] started RUNNING on worker[10.1.1.207:8091].
```

Timestamps above are from September 8, 2026; excerpts omit log prefixes and abbreviate the metadata line. This proves the shutdown call reached HRTR before assignment, rather than merely waiting in TaskQueue's asynchronous executor.

The subsequent sequence shows successive waves of cancelled work occupying capacity:

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 10:54:13.073 | New test task `index_kafka_datasource_diinaocp_6d1c6a3fba1682a_mpplelhh` enters HRTR pending state. |
| 10:54:46.801 | Reconciliation invokes HRTR shutdown again for old tasks, including `index_kafka_datasource_alifbaan_c8be674ffa9e8b8_mdlpbdho`. |
| 10:54:46.812 | HRTR assigns that already-cancelled task. Two more old tasks are assigned at `.819` and `.827`; all three are reported RUNNING by `.835`. |
| 10:55:46.800 onward | Reconciliation requests shutdown again. |
| 10:55:46.848 | One more cancelled old task is assigned. |
| 10:55:46.853 | The new test task finally gets assigned. |
| 10:55:47.091 | Autoscaler selects task count `4`. |

The new task's pending interval is **93.780 seconds**, about **95.1%** of the reported test duration. This strongly supports stale-task scheduling as the dominant delay. The exact runtime improvement still needs a fixed-code comparison; this report does not claim all test overhead would disappear.

### Why reconciliation does not prevent this

[TaskQueue.notifyStatus](https://github.com/FrankChen021/druid/blob/ef8090de9586daffc08c851528c092982e782384/indexing-service/src/main/java/org/apache/druid/indexing/overlord/TaskQueue.java#L710) marks the queue entry complete, persists terminal status, and asynchronously calls runner shutdown.

When a worker reports `RUNNING`, [taskAddedOrUpdated](https://github.com/FrankChen021/druid/blob/ef8090de9586daffc08c851528c092982e782384/indexing-service/src/main/java/org/apache/druid/indexing/overlord/hrtr/HttpRemoteTaskRunner.java#L1431) checks TaskStorage only if there is no in-memory item. The retained pending item therefore transitions to RUNNING without consulting the persisted failure. Later reconciliation can kill it now that it is RUNNING, but another pending cancelled task can take its slot.

### Case 2: PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN cancellation race

The assignment loop reserves a worker and sets `PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN` under `statusLock`, then releases the lock before calling `runTaskOnWorker()` / `WorkerHolder.assignTask()`.

A possible interleaving is:

1. Assignment thread selects the task and releases `statusLock`.
2. TaskQueue persists cancellation; HRTR receives shutdown while the item is `PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN` and takes no action.
3. The assignment thread sends the request, or an already-sent request completes.
4. A worker RUNNING announcement is accepted through the retained item.

This follows from the source, but the CI excerpts above do not prove cancellation occurred in this intermediate state. This case needs a latch-controlled regression test.

### Proposed staged fix and acceptance criteria

**First, narrowly fix exact `State.PENDING`:** under `statusLock`, detach the item from `tasks`, remove its ID from `pendingTaskIds`, and notify waiters. Outside the lock, complete the captured item's existing future through `taskComplete(item, null, TaskStatus.failure(taskId, reason))`.

Selection uses the same lock: if cancellation wins while strictly PENDING, the task cannot subsequently be selected. If selection wins, the item is PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN and belongs to the separate fix. Use exact state equality, not `isPending()`, for this staged change.

Do not pre-set COMPLETE and then invoke the current `setResult`, which attempts the same strict state transition again. Detaching first allows reuse of the existing completion path without that double transition. Preserve running-task completion callbacks and metrics.

**Separately handle in-flight assignment:** remember cancellation across dispatch and late announcements; check before dispatch; shut down an accepted task if cancellation races the request; prevent reverting a cancelled item to PENDING. - Cancel strictly PENDING with no capacity, then add capacity and a live task. Assert the cancelled task is never assigned and the live task progresses.
- Assert the cancelled item's original future completes with FAILED and the reason, its pending/known entries are removed, and repeated shutdown emits no duplicate terminal notification.
- Verify callbacks execute without `statusLock` held; simple same-thread reentry alone is insufficient because Java monitors are reentrant.
- Pause after selection and during assignment to exercise PENDING_WORKER_ASSIGN cancellation, late RUNNING, assignment rejection, and duplicate terminal announcements.
- Verify worker reservation cleanup with multiple assignment threads.
- Re-run the autoscaler class including preceding-test teardown; an isolated scale-up method does not reliably reproduce the cross-test backlog.

### Impact and related history

This uses production HRTR code. Plausible production consequences are wasted worker slots/resources, delayed valid tasks, and increased ingestion lag. CI directly demonstrates delayed scheduling; data corruption or duplicate publication has not been demonstrated.

#13558 changed shutdown from unconditional removal to retaining tasks except when COMPLETE, to preserve shutdown callbacks/metrics. It also introduced the existing `HttpRemoteTaskRunnerTest.testShutdown` assertion that a pending task remains known. That assertion does not verify cancellation or prevent later assignment. A wholesale revert risks restoring the original running-task callback issue.

No implementation changes or new test runs were performed for this report. Evidence consists of source inspection, historical patch inspection, and the downloaded CI artifact.

body_text:
### Affected version

Druid 27 with Calcite 1.21.0.

### Problem

A numeric `IN` predicate containing 11,481 literals causes a severe SQL planning slowdown:

```sql
maxLongUniform IN (11481 literal values)
```

A deterministic, planning-only JMH benchmark measured approximately **7,160 ms per plan** on Druid 27. The delay occurs during SQL planning, before native query execution.

### Root cause

For a literal list below `inSubQueryThreshold`, Calcite converts SQL `IN` into one equality per literal joined by `OR`:

```text
SQL IN
  -> 11,481 equality OR terms
  -> RexSimplify.simplifyOrTerms
  -> native IN filter optimization
```

Druid 27's legacy null-replacement mode exposes numeric columns as non-nullable to Calcite. This makes `simplifyOrTerms` accumulate prior equality terms as predicates while simplifying later terms, which scales poorly for thousands of values. Druid eventually combines the filters into a native `InDimFilter`, but only after Calcite has paid the simplification cost.

The SQL-to-OR rewrite is intentional. The defect is the scaling of cross-term predicate simplification for a very large equality disjunction. This is related to #7904 and [CALCITE-3178](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/CALCITE-3178).

### Version comparison

| Druid version | Calcite | Planning time |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Druid 27 | 1.21.0 | approximately 7,160 ms |
| Druid 32.0.0 | 1.37.0 | 25.322 +/- 5.677 ms |
| Current master | 1.42.0 | 27.814 +/- 6.485 ms |

The exact Druid 32.0.0 result was verified using the official Calcite 1.37.0 artifact and the same `maxLongUniform IN (11,481 literals)` query shape with `inSubQueryThreshold = Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

### Why Druid 32 and later are unaffected

Druid 32 removed legacy SQL-incompatible null handling in #17609. Ordinary numeric datasource columns are now exposed to Calcite as nullable. Calcite therefore skips the expensive predicate accumulation and can later combine the equality terms into `SEARCH/Sarg`.

The underlying Calcite weakness can still affect genuinely non-nullable schemas or plans where non-nullability is already established, but the original query against an ordinary Druid datasource does not reproduce the slowdown from Druid 32 onward.

### Suggested actions

- On Druid 27, set `inSubQueryThreshold` below the literal count so Calcite uses an inline `VALUES` relation instead of generating the large OR expression; validate the resulting execution plan.
- Upgrade to Druid 32 or later for the long-term resolution of this ordinary-datasource case.
- Retain a large-`IN` planning benchmark as a regression guard.


### Related Calcite allocation reductions

This is separate from the original Druid 27 numeric planning regression: these upstream changes reduce temporary allocation for large string `IN` predicates on Calcite 1.42.0.

| Calcite PR | Optimization | Allocation reduction (100,000 / 1,000,000 strings) |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| [#5280](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5280) | Avoid repeated generated-CAST resolution | 19.95% / 20.48% |
| [#5281](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5281) | Reuse unchanged character SQL types | 9.05% / 8.72% |
| [#5282](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5282) | Cache recently created and decorated SQL types | 45.74% / 44.70% |
| [#5283](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5283) | Copy SQL and Rex operands only when changed | 2.72% / 1.55% |
| [#5284](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5284) | Write Rex string literal digests directly | 2.46% / 1.31% |

The isolated reductions overlap and should not be added. With all five changes applied, allocation fell by 70.8% at 100,000 strings and 70.5% at 1,000,000 strings.

PR #20314 adds a separate planning-timeout guardrail that limits the Broker impact of pathological planning cases; it does not change the root cause described here.

Druid 27 with Calcite 1.21.0.

### Problem

A numeric `IN` predicate containing 11,481 literals causes a severe SQL planning slowdown:

```sql
maxLongUniform IN (11481 literal values)
```

A deterministic, planning-only JMH benchmark measured approximately **7,160 ms per plan** on Druid 27. The delay occurs during SQL planning, before native query execution.

### Root cause

For a literal list below `inSubQueryThreshold`, Calcite converts SQL `IN` into one equality per literal joined by `OR`:

```text
SQL IN
  -> 11,481 equality OR terms
  -> RexSimplify.simplifyOrTerms
  -> native IN filter optimization
```

Druid 27's legacy null-replacement mode exposes numeric columns as non-nullable to Calcite. This makes `simplifyOrTerms` accumulate prior equality terms as predicates while simplifying later terms, which scales poorly for thousands of values. Druid eventually combines the filters into a native `InDimFilter`, but only after Calcite has paid the simplification cost.

The SQL-to-OR rewrite is intentional. The defect is the scaling of cross-term predicate simplification for a very large equality disjunction. This is related to #7904 and [CALCITE-3178](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/CALCITE-3178).

### Version comparison

| Druid version | Calcite | Planning time |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Druid 27 | 1.21.0 | approximately 7,160 ms |
| Druid 32.0.0 | 1.37.0 | 25.322 +/- 5.677 ms |
| Current master | 1.42.0 | 27.814 +/- 6.485 ms |

The exact Druid 32.0.0 result was verified using the official Calcite 1.37.0 artifact and the same `maxLongUniform IN (11,481 literals)` query shape with `inSubQueryThreshold = Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

### Why Druid 32 and later are unaffected

Druid 32 removed legacy SQL-incompatible null handling in #17609. Ordinary numeric datasource columns are now exposed to Calcite as nullable. Calcite therefore skips the expensive predicate accumulation and can later combine the equality terms into `SEARCH/Sarg`.

The underlying Calcite weakness can still affect genuinely non-nullable schemas or plans where non-nullability is already established, but the original query against an ordinary Druid datasource does not reproduce the slowdown from Druid 32 onward.

### Suggested actions

- On Druid 27, set `inSubQueryThreshold` below the literal count so Calcite uses an inline `VALUES` relation instead of generating the large OR expression; validate the resulting execution plan.
- Upgrade to Druid 32 or later for the long-term resolution of this ordinary-datasource case.
- Retain a large-`IN` planning benchmark as a regression guard.


### Related Calcite allocation reductions

This is separate from the original Druid 27 numeric planning regression: these upstream changes reduce temporary allocation for large string `IN` predicates on Calcite 1.42.0.

| Calcite PR | Optimization | Allocation reduction (100,000 / 1,000,000 strings) |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| [#5280](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5280) | Avoid repeated generated-CAST resolution | 19.95% / 20.48% |
| [#5281](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5281) | Reuse unchanged character SQL types | 9.05% / 8.72% |
| [#5282](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5282) | Cache recently created and decorated SQL types | 45.74% / 44.70% |
| [#5283](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5283) | Copy SQL and Rex operands only when changed | 2.72% / 1.55% |
| [#5284](https://github.com/apache/calcite/pull/5284) | Write Rex string literal digests directly | 2.46% / 1.31% |

The isolated reductions overlap and should not be added. With all five changes applied, allocation fell by 70.8% at 100,000 strings and 70.5% at 1,000,000 strings.

body_text:
### Affected Version

Observed on 36.x; the relevant code paths are unchanged on `master` (as of commit `2bf1643cdd`). Uses the HTTP-based task runner (`druid.indexer.runner.type=httpRemote`).

### Summary

If a MiddleManager's node-discovery entry **flaps (removed then re-added) during the Overlord's startup worker-sync**, the Overlord's `becomeLeader()` blocks for the full `3 × druid.indexer.runner.syncRequestTimeout` (default `3 × PT3M = 9 minutes`) awaiting a stale `WorkerHolder` whose initialization latch can never fire, then throws and **fails leadership acquisition**. During that window the Overlord is effectively leaderless (no supervisor management), and the failure triggers a further leadership transition.

### Description

**Cluster / config**
- `httpRemote` task runner; combined Coordinator/Overlord process.
- ~12 MiddleManagers, ~40 Kafka streaming supervisors.
- `druid.indexer.runner.syncRequestTimeout` left at its default `PT3M`.
- ZooKeeper-based discovery (`CuratorDruidNodeDiscoveryProvider`).

**Trigger**
The ZooKeeper ensemble leader restarted, causing a brief re-election and Curator `SUSPENDED → RECONNECTED` on the Druid processes. This forced an Overlord leadership change. As the new leader ran `becomeLeader()`, one MiddleManager's ZK session had also reset, so its ephemeral discovery node was deleted and immediately re-created — a remove+add flap occurring within ~1s of the Overlord starting its worker sync.

**Observed behavior (timestamps relative)**
```
T+0.000  New leader: HttpRemoteTaskRunner - "[12] Workers are discovered."
T+0.000  ChangeRequestHttpSyncer - "Starting sync for server[...MM-X...]" (x12)
T+0.000  HttpRemoteTaskRunner - "Waiting for worker[MM-0] to sync state..."
T+1.017  HttpRemoteTaskRunner - "Kaboom! Worker[MM-X] removed!"      # old ZK node gone
T+1.350  HttpRemoteTaskRunner - "Worker[MM-X] reportin' for duty!"  # new ZK node -> new holder, syncs fine
T+1.359  HttpRemoteTaskRunner - "Task[...] location changed on worker[MM-X]"  # new holder healthy
...
T+555.4  ERROR CuratorDruidLeaderSelector - "listener becomeLeader() failed. Unable to become leader"
```

Stack trace (host scrubbed):
```
java.lang.RuntimeException: java.lang.RuntimeException: org.apache.druid.java.util.common.RE:
    Failed to sync with worker[<middlemanager-host>:8088].
	at org.apache.druid.indexing.overlord.DruidOverlord$1.becomeLeader(DruidOverlord.java)
	...
```

The block lasted ~555s ≈ `3 × PT3M` (540s) plus the time to await the earlier, healthy workers. The re-added MiddleManager was healthy the entire time (its new `WorkerHolder` synced within ~1s and streamed task snapshots); only the **stale, stopped holder** the startup loop was awaiting never initialized.

### Root cause

Leadership callbacks run on a single-threaded executor and `becomeLeader()` is invoked synchronously, so the whole node cannot process any further leadership transition until it returns:
- `CuratorDruidLeaderSelector#createNewLeaderLatchWithListener` — `isLeader()` calls `listener.becomeLeader()` inline on the `LeaderSelector[...]` single-thread executor; on any thrown exception it alerts and calls `notLeader()`.

`becomeLeader()` starts the task runner (a managed lifecycle instance) **before** the supervisor manager, and `HttpRemoteTaskRunner.start()` blocks until it has synced with every discovered worker:
- `DruidOverlord$1.becomeLeader()` builds the `"task-master"` `Lifecycle`, adds `taskRunner` (`HttpRemoteTaskRunner`) as a managed instance, then `supervisorManager`, then `leaderLifecycle.start()`.
- `HttpRemoteTaskRunner#startWorkersHandling()` — after worker discovery, iterates `for (WorkerHolder worker : workers.values()) { worker.waitForInitialization(); }`. The loop holds `WorkerHolder` references obtained at loop start.

The per-worker wait can never complete for a flapped worker:
- `WorkerHolder#waitForInitialization()` → `syncer.awaitInitialization()`; returns `false` → `throw new RE("Failed to sync with worker[%s]")`.
- `ChangeRequestHttpSyncer`: `maxDurationToWaitForSync = 3 * serverHttpTimeout` and `awaitInitialization()` awaits `initializationLatch` up to that duration. `serverHttpTimeout` is `HttpRemoteTaskRunnerConfig#getSyncRequestTimeout()` (default `PT3M`). **`initializationLatch` is only counted down on the first successful full/delta sync.**
- When the worker's discovery node is removed, `HttpRemoteTaskRunner#removeWorker()` does `workers.remove(host)` then `workerHolder.stop()` → `syncer.stop()`. **Stopping the syncer does not count down `initializationLatch`.**

So when the node flaps mid-startup: the old holder the startup loop is awaiting gets `stop()`ped (latch stuck at 1 forever), while a brand-new holder is created via `addWorker()` and syncs normally. The loop keeps awaiting the **dead** holder, blocks the full `3 × syncRequestTimeout`, then throws — failing `becomeLeader()`.

### Impact

- Overlord leadership acquisition is delayed/failed for up to `3 × druid.indexer.runner.syncRequestTimeout` (default **9 minutes**) whenever a worker's discovery entry flaps during that startup window — likely during the very ZK instability that caused the leadership change in the first place.
- During the gap the Overlord never reaches `SupervisorManager.start()`, so streaming supervisors are unmanaged: Kafka indexing tasks that reach their `taskDuration` and exit are not replaced, and ingestion falls behind. When leadership finally settles on another node, all supervisors are (re)started at once, producing a synchronized ingestion-lag spike across every datasource on the cluster.
- The `becomeLeader()` failure calls `notLeader()`, adding another leadership transition to an already-unstable moment.

### Suggested fixes (for discussion)

1. In `startWorkersHandling()`, don't await a captured `WorkerHolder` reference — re-check the current holder in `workers` (skip/replace ones that have been removed/stopped), or await by host and drop the wait if the entry disappears.
2. Have `WorkerHolder#stop()` / `ChangeRequestHttpSyncer#stop()` count down (or otherwise release) `initializationLatch` so `awaitInitialization()` returns promptly for a stopped syncer instead of blocking the full timeout.
3. Make the initial worker sync best-effort: log-and-continue when a single worker can't sync at startup (it will sync via the normal `addWorker` path) rather than failing the entire `becomeLeader()` — optionally bound the aggregate wait rather than paying `3 × syncRequestTimeout` per worker.

### Debugging already done

Correlated Overlord logs (`becomeLeader` start → `becomeLeader() failed` after ~555s with `Failed to sync with worker[...]`), the affected MiddleManager's logs (process healthy throughout; ZK node re-announced; successfully POSTing to the new Overlord), and the discovery flap on the Overlord (`Kaboom! Worker[...] removed!` then `reportin' for duty!` within ~1s), against the code paths above. Timing matches `3 × PT3M`.

- `HttpRemoteTaskRunner#startWorkersHandling()` — after worker discovery, iterates `for (WorkerHolder worker : workers.values()) { worker.waitForInitialization(); }`. The loop holds `WorkerHolder` references obtained at loop start.

The per-worker wait can never complete for a flapped worker:
- `WorkerHolder#waitForInitialization()` → `syncer.awaitInitialization()`; returns `false` → `throw new RE("Failed to sync with worker[%s]")`.
- `ChangeRequestHttpSyncer`: `maxDurationToWaitForSync = 3 * serverHttpTimeout` and `awaitInitialization()` awaits `initializationLatch` up to that duration. `serverHttpTimeout` is `HttpRemoteTaskRunnerConfig#getSyncRequestTimeout()` (default `PT3M`). **`initializationLatch` is only counted down on the first successful full/delta sync.**
- When the worker's discovery node is removed, `HttpRemoteTaskRunner#removeWorker()` does `workers.remove(host)` then `workerHolder.stop()` → `syncer.stop()`. **Stopping the syncer does not count down `initializationLatch`.**

So when the node flaps mid-startup: the old holder the startup loop is awaiting gets `stop()`ped (latch stuck at 1 forever), while a brand-new holder is created via `addWorker()` and syncs normally. The loop keeps awaiting the **dead** holder, blocks the full `3 × syncRequestTimeout`, then throws — failing `becomeLeader()`.

### Impact

- Overlord leadership acquisition is delayed/failed for up to `3 × druid.indexer.runner.syncRequestTimeout` (default **9 minutes**) whenever a worker's discovery entry flaps during that startup window — likely during the very ZK instability that caused the leadership change in the first place.
- During the gap the Overlord never reaches `SupervisorManager.start()`, so streaming supervisors are unmanaged: Kafka indexing tasks that reach their `taskDuration` and exit are not replaced, and ingestion falls behind. When leadership finally settles on another node, all supervisors are (re)started at once, producing a synchronized ingestion-lag spike across every datasource on the cluster.
- The `becomeLeader()` failure calls `notLeader()`, adding another leadership transition to an already-unstable moment.

### Suggested fixes (for discussion)

1. In `startWorkersHandling()`, don't await a captured `WorkerHolder` reference — re-check the current holder in `workers` (skip/replace ones that have been removed/stopped), or await by host and drop the wait if the entry disappears.
2. Have `WorkerHolder#stop()` / `ChangeRequestHttpSyncer#stop()` count down (or otherwise release) `initializationLatch` so `awaitInitialization()` returns promptly for a stopped syncer instead of blocking the full timeout.
3. Make the initial worker sync best-effort: log-and-continue when a single worker can't sync at startup (it will sync via the normal `addWorker` path) rather than failing the entire `becomeLeader()` — optionally bound the aggregate wait rather than paying `3 × syncRequestTimeout` per worker.

### Debugging already done

Correlated Overlord logs (`becomeLeader` start → `becomeLeader() failed` after ~555s with `Failed to sync with worker[...]`), the affected MiddleManager's logs (process healthy throughout; ZK node re-announced; successfully POSTing to the new Overlord), and the discovery flap on the Overlord (`Kaboom! Worker[...] removed!` then `reportin' for duty!` within ~1s), against the code paths above. Timing matches `3 × PT3M`.

### Description

PR #19510 added an opt-in Iceberg Arrow reader, but the native batch-ingestion boundary is still row-oriented. `IcebergArrowInputSourceReader` currently converts every Arrow `ColumnarBatch` row into a `Map<String, Object>` and `MapBasedInputRow`. `InputSourceReader` then exposes `CloseableIterator<InputRow>`, `InputSourceProcessor` loops over individual rows, and `IncrementalIndex.add` accepts one `InputRow` at a time.

This issue proposes carrying the columnar representation deeper into native batch ingestion so Arrow decoding gains are not lost to per-row materialization before indexing.

### Motivation

Local JMH results after #19510 show the bottleneck moving downstream:

- Reader-only workloads are 1.23–1.58x faster, with a 1.36x geomean.
- End-to-end `read -> incremental index -> segment persist` is 1.02x faster .


### Acceptance criteria

- Existing row-based input sources and ingestion specifications remain compatible.
- The batch path demonstrates a statistically significant end-to-end improvement on at least one representative wide-table workload without regressing the TPC-H `lineitem` case.
- Unsupported operations fall back clearly to the row path rather than changing results.

### Root cause

`K3sClusterResource.waitUntilPodIsReady` waits 300 s for each pod's `Ready=True` condition. On timeout it throws an ISE that contains only the pod name. **Failures:** 2 · **First seen:** 2026-09-23 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-10

### Root cause

After the stream is resharded from 2 to 4 shards, the supervisor must finish the closed shards, publish, and start tasks on the child shards. On a busy runner, `ingest/rows/published` did not reach 2000 within 240 s, and the timeout message does not say whether the tasks were stuck or just slow. The 2026-10-10 failure was on a Dependabot bump of `amazon-kinesis-client` (#20533), but the same job passed on the two later master commits that include that bump.

### Suggested fix

Wait for the supervisor to report 4 partitions before waiting on the row aggregate, and log the supervisor status and the current row sum on timeout.

_This issue was generated automatically by Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent) running a scheduled CI-triage routine on behalf of @FrankChen021. Analysis and suggested fixes are AI-produced; please verify before acting on them._

**Status:** Open: recurred after #20459
**Subject:** Maven project-model build aborts before any test runs (any Maven job)
**Failures:** 11 · **First seen:** 2026-09-23 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-21

### Root cause

Maven aborts building the project model because it cannot fetch the parent POM `org.apache:apache:pom:NN` from Maven Central. Earlier failures fell back to a repository declared with unresolved `${repoOrgUrl}` placeholders; on 2026-10-08 Central itself answered not-found for `org.apache:apache:pom:40` on a runner with no `~/.m2` cache, three times in about 25 s, while every other job in the same run resolved it. On 2026-10-16 it happened twice more, 11 hours apart; in the `strict-compilation` job the parent POM resolved on the third attempt but the checkstyle plugin's dependency descriptors then also came back not-found, so the miss is not limited to the parent POM. On 2026-10-17 two more jobs on different commits, started within a minute of each other, failed all 3 attempts the same way. On 2026-10-20 Central's CDN returned HTTP 502 for ordinary dependency POMs mid-build, which Maven then cached as a failure for the rest of the run. On 2026-10-21 Central also answered HTTP 429 (rate limited) to two jobs, once for the parent POM and once for a surefire provider POM mid-build. It is a transient Central/CDN miss, unrelated to the commits.

### Suggested fix

#20459 added a 3-attempt `./mvnw -N validate` pre-resolve step, which is not enough. Use a longer exponential backoff (e.g. 5 attempts up to ~2 minutes) in that step, and always restore a small `~/.m2` cache that holds `org.apache:apache` so the job doesn't depend on a fresh Central download. For mid-build misses, raise the resolver's HTTP retry count (`-Daether.connector.http.retryHandler.count=5` on Maven 3.9, in `.mvn/maven.config`) so 5xx and 429 responses are retried instead of cached as failures.

_This issue was generated automatically by Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent) running a scheduled CI-triage routine on behalf of @FrankChen021. Analysis and suggested fixes are AI-produced; please verify before acting on them._

**Status:** Open: no fix PR
**Subject:** `.github/scripts/setup_generate_license.sh` `apt-get update` hang (Static Checks CI, `packaging-check (25) / packaging-check-jdk25`)
**Failures:** 1 · **First seen:** 2026-10-01 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-01

### Root cause

`packaging-check.sh` first runs `setup_generate_license.sh`, which calls `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install python3 -y` with no timeout. On 87d36ea342 the runner's `azure.archive.ubuntu.com` mirror was ignored, apt fell back to `archive.ubuntu.com`, and the update stalled after fetching `noble-security InRelease` with no further output until the 60-minute step timeout killed the job. This is a runner/mirror outage, unrelated to the commit (a dependency-classloader change); the same job compiled normally on neighbouring commits.

### Suggested fix

Skip the apt step when `python3 -m venv` and `pip3` already work (the `ubuntu-24.04` runner image ships Python 3), or bound it with `timeout 300 sudo apt-get -o Acquire::Retries=3 -o Acquire::http::Timeout=30 update` so a stalled mirror fails fast.

### Occurrences

Failed push-triggered master jobs only. The daily triage routine adds one row per new failed job.

| Date | Commit | Job | Failure log | Detail | Reported in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-01 | 87d36ea342 (#20468) | `packaging-check (25) / packaging-check-jdk25` | [job 110455920873](https://github.com/apache/druid/actions/runs/36887937082/job/110455920873) | `apt-get update` in `setup_generate_license.sh` hung after fetching `noble-security InRelease`; step killed at 60-minute timeout | |

The Broker runs a query itself, through LocalQuerySegmentWalker, when all of its datasources are global (e.g. inline, lookup, subquery, etc). On this path the Broker uses the same per-segment engines as data servers, but running on the query thread (the HTTP request handling thread) rather than a bounded processing pool. This can lead to excessive allocation of processing buffers, to the degree that the query engines request them.

As a workaround, people can lower `druid.processing.buffer.sizeBytes` or raise `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize` on Brokers. If doing the first, it may be useful to also enable disk spilling with `druid.query.groupBy.maxOnDiskStorage`.

Possible fixes:

1. Give the Broker a bounded-size local processing pool, and run processing tasks there rather than in HTTP threads.
2. Allocate processing buffers by slicing up merge buffers, rather than allocating from an on-demand processing buffer pool. (Queries would wait for buffers to become available.)

Druid currently has 1,911 open CodeQL `java/deprecated-call` alerts across 579 files. Most occur in test sources, but 488 are in production sources.

[CodeQL alerts](https://github.com/apache/druid/security/code-scanning?query=is%3Aopen+branch%3Amaster+rule%3Ajava%2Fdeprecated-call)

This issue tracks migrating deprecated API calls, removing obsolete internal Druid APIs, and adding enforcement where practical. The counts below reflect the alert inventory retrieved on October 8, 2026, and may change as fixes land.

### Major cleanup areas

| API group | Alerts |
|---|---:|
| SQL expression test helpers | 470 |
| `DataSegment` constructors and no-argument `builder()` | 420 |
| `URL` constructors | 101 |
| Calcite rule operand APIs | 95 |
| `SeekableStreamSupervisorSpec.getDataSchema()` | 52 |
| `JvmUtils.getRuntimeInfo()` | 47 |
| Guava `Throwables` methods | 43 |
| `QueryRunnerFactory.mergeRunners(ExecutorService, …)` | 41 |

### Proposed approach

**Druid APIs**

Migrate callers to the supported replacements and remove deprecated internal declarations in the same change.

Removal candidates should be outside the API surface protected by `@PublicApi` or `@ExtensionPoint`. Check annotations on individual members and contracts inherited from parent classes or interfaces, as well as annotations on the declaring class.

Separately review methods used by serialization, configuration, HTTP endpoints, persisted metadata, reflection, or dependency injection. These may have compatibility requirements even without either annotation.

**Dependency and JDK APIs**

Follow the replacement guidance for each dependency while preserving behavior. Split the work into focused PRs by API family or module.

For deprecated `URL` constructors:

- Replace ordinary construction with `URI` followed by `toURL()`.
- Use `Path.toUri()` or `File.toURI()` for filesystem paths.
- Review relative URLs, escaping, exception handling, and custom `URLStreamHandler` usage.
- Add all deprecated URL constructor overloads to `codestyle/druid-forbidden-apis.txt` to prevent regressions.

### Cases requiring care

- `DataSegment.builder(SegmentId)` has different defaults from the deprecated no-argument builder. Preserve existing values where necessary.
- SQL expression tests should compare complete typed `DruidExpression` structures when migrating away from deprecated helpers.
- Compatibility bridges in extension APIs require an explicit compatibility decision before removal.
- Replacing `ResourcePool` finalization requires preserving resource cleanup behavior.
- Hashing changes must preserve compatibility with existing partition assignments and persisted identifiers.
- Guava exception propagation replacements must preserve checked exceptions, unchecked exceptions, and null handling.

### Completion criteria

- [ ] Migrate deprecated calls in focused batches.
- [ ] Remove deprecated internal Druid APIs that no longer need compatibility support.
- [ ] Add forbidden API rules for deprecated URL constructors.
- [ ] Run affected tests and static checks for each batch.
- [ ] Confirm resolved alerts after CodeQL rescans.
- [ ] Document any retained deprecated calls and the specific reason for retaining them.

Blanket suppression or removing deprecation annotations solely to silence warnings should not be used to resolve this issue.

### Root cause

About 15 s after `EmbeddedSecureJdbcDriverTest` started its embedded cluster, the surefire fork exited with code 1 and no test result, so surefire reported "The forked VM terminated without properly saying goodbye". A JVM crash or an OOM would give a different exit code. Code 1 matches the in-process `System.exit(1)` paths that embedded servers can reach: the Curator unhandled-error listener in `CuratorModule` and `CuratorDruidLeaderSelector.notLeader()`. All embedded servers share the surefire JVM, so either path kills the whole fork. The commit (#20524, ZooKeeper 3.8.6 → 3.8.7) is probably not the cause, because the next two master commits also use 3.8.7 and the job passed on both.

### Suggested fix

In the embedded-test harness, replace the JVM-exiting actions with ones that fail the test instead: inject `CuratorModule`'s `exitAction`, and route `CuratorDruidLeaderSelector`'s exit through an injectable hook. The root error then appears as a test failure with server logs. Until then, check the `*.dumpstream` in the run's `unit-test-reports-jdk25-*` artifact to confirm which path ran.

### Root cause

The class started at 21:19 UTC and never reported a result; the job step was killed at its 60-minute timeout about 43 minutes later. Every test method has `@Timeout(60)`, so the hang is outside test methods: most likely cluster shutdown in `@AfterAll` blocked on a Dart controller that keeps retrying `/workOrder` after `test_getQueryReport_forRunningAndCanceledQuery` cancels a query (the scenario #20313 describes), or the `@BeforeAll` ingestion wait. The commit (#20541) only changes v10 segment and projection capability handling, not Dart, and the same job passed on the next master commits.

### Suggested fix

#20313 (merged 2026-10-15) cancels active `/workOrder` futures when a worker is stopped, which should remove the hang. Also consider bounding lifecycle methods (for example `junit.jupiter.execution.timeout.lifecycle.method.default` in embedded-tests) so any future hang fails the class with a thread dump instead of consuming the whole job.

**Status:** Fix PR #20608 open
**Subject:** `KafkaClusterMetricsTest` (`test_ingest10kRows_ofSelfClusterMetrics_andVerifyValues`, `test_ingestClusterMetrics_withConcurrentCompactionSupervisor_andKillUnusedSegments`) (embedded-tests, `unit tests / unit tests(main) (25, K*,U*,Z*,Y*,X*)`)
**Failures:** 2 · **First seen:** 2026-10-14 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-21

### Root cause

Both tests timed out after the 60 s `useDefaultTimeoutForLatchableEmitter(60)`: one waiting for 10 `ingest/handoff/count` events (line 181), the other (MSQ compaction variant) waiting for the first `task/success/count` (line 229). The tests ingest the cluster's own metrics through the Kafka emitter, so their progress depends on the metric emission rate and on task scheduling on a busy runner. In the same job, the preceding `KinesisFaultToleranceTest` also failed on slow publishing. The commit (#20577) only bumps GitHub Actions versions, the re-run attempt passed this class in 68 s, and the next master commit was green. On 2026-10-21 the MSQ compaction variant instead timed out later, at line 317 waiting for the first `segment/kill/deepStorageSkipped/count`; the same job passed on every later master commit that ran its tests.

### Suggested fix

Review and land #20608 for the handoff stall: it traces the stalled handoff to a lost wakeup in `SegmentLoadDropHandler.processBatch()`, where a load that finishes before the batch future is registered leaves the Historical idle until the 5-minute `hostTimeout`. It fixes this by re-checking statuses under the `waitingFutures` lock. The kill-path wait (line 317) depends on kill-duty scheduling within 60 s; give that wait a longer timeout or shorten the kill period in the test's Overlord config.

_This issue was generated automatically by Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding agent) running a scheduled CI-triage routine on behalf of @FrankChen021. Analysis and suggested fixes are AI-produced; please verify before acting on them._

**Status:** Resolved by #20651
**Subject:** `KafkaIndexFaultToleranceTest.test_supervisorRecovers_afterCoordinatorRestart` (embedded-tests, `unit tests / unit tests(main) (25, K*,U*,Z*,Y*,X*)`)
**Failures:** 20 · **First seen:** 2026-10-14 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-21

### Root cause

Regression from #20505 (merged 2026-10-14 as 7c89096bd1), which makes the Overlord hold a streaming task's publish until earlier task groups on the same partitions finish. The Coordinator restart delays handoff past the test's completion timeout; the supervisor kills the earlier group and stops the later one, then marks the earlier group done, which releases the later task's held publish. The Overlord commits that task's segments and offsets, but the task is interrupted before it sees the result and never emits `ingest/rows/published`, so the metric stays short of 3000 and `verifyAndTearDown` times out. Since #20505 it has failed on 19 master commits (7 of 8 on 2026-10-20), always as the only failing test; the data itself is correct. Diagnosis from #20651.

### Suggested fix

Fixed by #20651: when the supervisor stops or kills a task (`killTask`, `killTaskWithSuccess`, `stopTask`), it first answers the task's held publish with "not ready", so a later release from the completed group has no effect. Merged on 2026-10-21 as 587e781a1b; the test has passed on every master commit since.

**Subject:** `ReservoirSegmentSamplerTest.testSegmentsFromMorePopulousServerAreMoreLikelyToBePicked` (server, `unit tests / unit tests(main) (25, R*,B*,P*)`)
**Failures:** 0 · **First seen:** 2026-10-16 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-20

### Root cause

The test runs `ReservoirSegmentSampler.pickMovableSegmentsFrom` 50 times over 1000 segments and asserts each server's share of picks within ±2% of the total. At the 5% sample size only 2500 segments are picked, so the tolerance is ±50 against a standard deviation of about 24 for server0 and 20 for the other servers (≈2.1σ and 2.6σ). About 5% of runs fail on the first attempt. Both occurrences are in the 5% case (1061 vs 1000, 552 vs 500), the sampler itself is behaving correctly, and neither commit touches the coordinator. So far each one has passed on the surefire retry.

### Suggested fix

Scale the tolerance with the sample size instead of a fixed 2%, e.g. `error = 4 * Math.sqrt(totalSegmentsPicked * p * (1 - p))` with `p` = 0.4 for server0 and 0.2 otherwise, or use more iterations for the 5% and 10% cases.

**Failures:** 1 · **First seen:** 2026-10-19 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-19

### Root cause

The test starts two coordinators (`coordinator1` and `coordinator2`) at the same time but assumes `coordinator1` wins the leader election: it waits for `segment/loadQueue/success` on `coordinator1.latchableEmitter()` (line 89) and later stops `coordinator1` to "switch" leaders. Only the leader runs the `HistoricalManagementDuties` that emit this metric, so when `coordinator2` wins the election, the wait times out after 10 s (`ISE: Timed out waiting for event after [10,000]ms`). ## Summary

The default unauthenticated Druid Router `POST /druid/v2/sql/` path materializes attacker-controlled SQL request bodies before processing. 

## Affected Project

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Project | `apache/druid` |
| Entry | `POST /druid/v2/sql/ on Druid Router HTTP port 8888` |
| Required privilege | anonymous |
| Suggested CVSS 3.1 | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` |

## Technical Details

- Trigger shape: Send progressively larger `text/plain` SQL bodies to the Router SQL endpoint; the failing local sample used a 512 MiB body.
- Root cause summary: The `SqlQuery.from` path reads the full input stream with `IOUtils.toByteArray(request.getInputStream())` and constructs a full string without a default body-size cap.
- Exploitation conditions: Router is reachable anonymously; no account is required; no proxy or Druid setting rejects large bodies below the failure threshold.

**Failures:** 2 · **First seen:** 2026-10-21 · **Last seen:** 2026-10-24

### Root cause

The test's `HistoricalBlackhole` stops the Historical's Jetty connector, binds a plain `ServerSocket` on the same fixed port (8083) to swallow `/workOrder` requests, and in `close()` closes that socket and calls `connector.start()` to rebind 8083. The rebind failed with `BindException: Address already in use` (line 190, via line 103): the port is released and re-acquired with no retry, and `close()` calls `executor.shutdownNow()` without waiting for the accept thread, so anything still holding 0.0.0.0:8083 at that instant fails the test. Neither failing commit touches this code (#20648 changes OpenTelemetry emitter packaging, #20675 bumps Vert.x), and the same job passed on the neighbouring master commits.

### Suggested fix

Avoid swapping the port: blackhole `/workOrder` and `/stop` with a Jetty handler or servlet filter on the Historical instead of stopping its connector. Failing that, await the accept thread's termination in `close()` and retry `connector.start()` with a short backoff on `BindException`.

### Pre-check

- [x] All content is in English.
- [x] I searched existing issues and pull requests for ActiveLimitFilter, ExecuteLimitFilter, active count, and limit-exception cleanup.

### Apache Dubbo Component

Java SDK (apache/dubbo), dubbo-rpc-api filters and the dubbo-cluster filter chain.

### Dubbo Version

3.3.7-SNAPSHOT, branch `3.3` at `dab47b7843`; Windows, OpenJDK 17.0.17, Maven 3.9.4.

### Steps to reproduce this issue

Both concurrency filters skip `RpcStatus.endCount()` whenever their error listener receives a `RpcException` with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED_EXCEPTION`. This correctly skips cleanup when the filter itself rejects admission, but also skips it when admission succeeded and a downstream invoker throws that exception (or its response future completes exceptionally with it).

A minimal synchronous reproduction in a test in `dubbo-cluster` (JUnit 5 / Mockito; ordinary imports omitted):

```java
URL url = URL.valueOf("test://localhost:12345/limit-repro?actives=1&timeout=1");
Invoker<Object> target = mock(Invoker.class);
when(target.getUrl()).thenReturn(url);
when(target.getInterface()).thenReturn(Object.class);
when(target.invoke(any())).thenThrow(
        new RpcException(RpcException.LIMIT_EXCEEDED_EXCEPTION, "downstream rejected"));

Filter filter = new ActiveLimitFilter();
```

### Apache Dubbo Component

Java SDK (apache/dubbo)

### Dubbo Version

Dubbo Java 3.3.7-SNAPSHOT, OpenJDK 21.0.10, Windows 11 (x86_64)

### Steps to reproduce this issue

BatchExecutorQueue takes a snapshot of everything currently queued and processes each item in turn. If one item's prepare() or flush() throws, the exception propagates out and the rest of the snapshot is never processed, even though those items were already removed from the queue. TripleWriteQueue, which extends BatchExecutorQueue in dubbo-rpc-triple, only catches CompletionException around these calls, so any other exception — a NullPointerException or IllegalStateException, for example — escapes and drops the remaining commands in that batch. Since the queue is shared across all streams of one TripleInvoker, a single failing command can affect other, unrelated calls on the same invoker.


### What you expected to happen

When one queued item fails, every other item in the same batch should still be processed. The failing item should fail on its own without affecting the rest, and for TripleWriteQueue the failing command's associated result must be completed with the failure rather than left permanently incomplete.

A Kotlin project with a single dependency on `org.apache.dubbo:dubbo:3.3.6`. No provider,

```kotlin
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20"
    application
}
```

### Pre-check

- [x] I am sure that all the content I provide is in English.


### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/dubbo/issues?q=is%3Aissue) and found no similar issues.


### Apache Dubbo Component

Java SDK (apache/dubbo)

### Dubbo Version

Dubbo Java 3.3.6, OpenJDK 21 (Amazon Corretto 21.0.5), macOS 15.6 (OS-independent)
Kotlin 2.4.20, Gradle 9.5, default hessian2 serialization

### Steps to reproduce this issue


A Kotlin project with one Dubbo dependency. Provider and consumer run in the same JVM over a real
Netty `dubbo://` transport with a direct URL and `RegistryConfig("N/A")`, so no registry or other
infrastructure is needed — and because the transport is real rather than `injvm://`, values are
genuinely serialized.

`build.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20"
    application
}
repositories { mavenCentral() }
dependencies {
    implementation("org.apache.dubbo:dubbo:3.3.6")
    implementation("io.netty:netty-all:4.1.118.Final")
    implementation("org.javassist:javassist:3.30.2-GA")
    implementation("org.slf4j:slf4j-simple:2.0.13")
}
kotlin { jvmToolchain(21) }
application { mainClass = "repro.MainKt" }
```

`src/main/resources/security/serialize.allowlist`:

```
repro
```

`src/main/kotlin/Main.kt`:

```kotlin
package repro

import java.io.Serializable
import org.apache.dubbo.config.*
import org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap

sealed interface Reply : Serializable

data class Found(val text: String) : Reply

object NotFoundObject : Reply          // equals() is inherited identity comparison
data object NotFoundDataObject : Reply // compiler generates equals()
enum class NotFoundEnum : Reply { INSTANCE }

interface ReplyService {
    fun roundTrip(reply: Reply): Reply // returns its argument unchanged
}

class ReplyServiceImpl : ReplyService {
    override fun roundTrip(reply: Reply): Reply = reply
}

/** The dispatch a consumer actually writes. */
private fun describe(reply: Reply): String = when (reply) {
    NotFoundObject -> "matched NotFoundObject"
    NotFoundDataObject -> "matched NotFoundDataObject"
    NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE -> "matched NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE"
    is Found -> "matched Found(${reply.text})"
    else -> ">>> FELL THROUGH TO else <<<"
}

private fun report(label: String, sent: Reply, back: Reply) =
    println("%-12s | ===:%-5s | ==:%-5s | %s".format(label, back === sent, back == sent, describe(back)))

fun main() {
    DubboBootstrap.getInstance()
        .application(ApplicationConfig("repro"))
        .registry(RegistryConfig("N/A"))
        .protocol(ProtocolConfig("dubbo", 20881))
        .service(ServiceConfig<ReplyService>().apply {
            setInterface(ReplyService::class.java)
            setRef(ReplyServiceImpl())
        })
        .start()

    val svc = ReferenceConfig<ReplyService>().apply {
        setInterface(ReplyService::class.java)
        url = "dubbo://127.0.0.1:20881"
    }.get()

    report("object", NotFoundObject, svc.roundTrip(NotFoundObject))
    report("data object", NotFoundDataObject, svc.roundTrip(NotFoundDataObject))
    report("enum", NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE, svc.roundTrip(NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE))
    report("data class", Found("hi"), svc.roundTrip(Found("hi")))

    DubboBootstrap.getInstance().destroy()
}
```

`./gradlew run` prints:

```
object       | ===:false | ==:false | >>> FELL THROUGH TO else <<<
data object  | ===:false | ==:true  | matched NotFoundDataObject
enum         | ===:true  | ==:true  | matched NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE
data class   | ===:false | ==:true  | matched Found(hi)
```


### What you expected to happen

**Expected:** `NotFoundObject` should arrive at the consumer as the singleton, so the
`NotFoundObject ->` branch runs — the same way an enum constant survives today.

**Actual:** it arrives as a *different instance of the same class*, the `when` matches nothing, and
control reaches `else`. No exception, no warning, no log line — only the wrong code path.

Kotlin's `object` declares a singleton: the compiler emits a final class with a **private**
constructor and a single `public static final INSTANCE`, and the language guarantees no other
instance exists. The default bean deserializers do not honour that — they allocate a fresh instance,
bypassing the private constructor, and populate its fields. So Dubbo produces an instance the
language says cannot exist.

Because a plain `object` inherits `equals` from `Any` (identity comparison), losing identity also
loses equality, and Kotlin's `when` compares with `==`. That is why dispatch silently changes.

Hessian2 already solves exactly this problem for the Java equivalent. `EnumDeserializer` writes the
constant's name and resolves the real JVM constant on the way back, which is why the `enum` row
above is intact including `===`. A Kotlin `object` is just a class with a static `INSTANCE` and gets
no such treatment.

```
repro
```

`src/main/kotlin/Main.kt`:

```kotlin
package repro

import java.io.Serializable
import org.apache.dubbo.config.*
import org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap

sealed interface Reply : Serializable

data class Found(val text: String) : Reply

object NotFoundObject : Reply          // equals() is inherited identity comparison
data object NotFoundDataObject : Reply // compiler generates equals()
enum class NotFoundEnum : Reply { INSTANCE }

interface ReplyService {
    fun roundTrip(reply: Reply): Reply // returns its argument unchanged
}

class ReplyServiceImpl : ReplyService {
    override fun roundTrip(reply: Reply): Reply = reply
}

/** The dispatch a consumer actually writes. */
private fun describe(reply: Reply): String = when (reply) {
    NotFoundObject -> "matched NotFoundObject"
    NotFoundDataObject -> "matched NotFoundDataObject"
    NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE -> "matched NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE"
    is Found -> "matched Found(${reply.text})"
    else -> ">>> FELL THROUGH TO else <<<"
}

private fun report(label: String, sent: Reply, back: Reply) =
    println("%-12s | ===:%-5s | ==:%-5s | %s".format(label, back === sent, back == sent, describe(back)))

fun main() {
    DubboBootstrap.getInstance()
        .application(ApplicationConfig("repro"))
        .registry(RegistryConfig("N/A"))
        .protocol(ProtocolConfig("dubbo", 20881))
        .service(ServiceConfig<ReplyService>().apply {
            setInterface(ReplyService::class.java)
            setRef(ReplyServiceImpl())
        })
        .start()

    val svc = ReferenceConfig<ReplyService>().apply {
        setInterface(ReplyService::class.java)
        url = "dubbo://127.0.0.1:20881"
    }.get()

    report("object", NotFoundObject, svc.roundTrip(NotFoundObject))
    report("data object", NotFoundDataObject, svc.roundTrip(NotFoundDataObject))
    report("enum", NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE, svc.roundTrip(NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE))
    report("data class", Found("hi"), svc.roundTrip(Found("hi")))

    DubboBootstrap.getInstance().destroy()
}
```

`./gradlew run` prints:

```
object       | ===:false | ==:false | >>> FELL THROUGH TO else <<<
data object  | ===:false | ==:true  | matched NotFoundDataObject
enum         | ===:true  | ==:true  | matched NotFoundEnum.INSTANCE
data class   | ===:false | ==:true  | matched Found(hi)
```


### What you expected to happen

**Expected:** `NotFoundObject` should arrive at the consumer as the singleton, so the
`NotFoundObject ->` branch runs — the same way an enum constant survives today.

**Actual:** it arrives as a *different instance of the same class*, the `when` matches nothing, and
control reaches `else`. No exception, no warning, no log line — only the wrong code path.

Kotlin's `object` declares a singleton: the compiler emits a final class with a **private**
constructor and a single `public static final INSTANCE`, and the language guarantees no other
instance exists. The default bean deserializers do not honour that — they allocate a fresh instance,
bypassing the private constructor, and populate its fields. So Dubbo produces an instance the
language says cannot exist.

Because a plain `object` inherits `equals` from `Any` (identity comparison), losing identity also
loses equality, and Kotlin's `when` compares with `==`. That is why dispatch silently changes.

Hessian2 already solves exactly this problem for the Java equivalent. `EnumDeserializer` writes the
constant's name and resolves the real JVM constant on the way back, which is why the `enum` row
above is intact including `===`. A Kotlin `object` is just a class with a static `INSTANCE` and gets
no such treatment.

### Pre-check

- [x] I am sure that all the content I provide is in English.


### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/dubbo/issues?q=is%3Aissue) and found no similar issues.


### Apache Dubbo Component

Java SDK (apache/dubbo)

### Dubbo Version

Dubbo Java 3.3.6, OpenJDK 21 (Amazon Corretto 21.0.5), macOS 15.6 (OS-independent)
Kotlin 2.4.20 / Java 17+ sealed types, Gradle 9.5, default hessian2 serialization, STRICT mode

### Steps to reproduce this issue

`SerializeSecurityConfigurator.registerInterface` auto-allow-lists the classes it can reach from an
exported interface's signatures. `checkClass` walks **up** into supertypes and **into** fields and
generic arguments, but never **down** into subtypes. A sealed parameter or return type therefore
gets the parent trusted and none of the subtypes that actually travel on the wire.

This is the default configuration — `autoTrustSerializeClass` defaults to `true` and the check
status to `STRICT` — and **no `security/serialize.allowlist` file is supplied below**.

Provider and consumer run in one JVM over a real Netty `dubbo://` transport with a direct URL and
`RegistryConfig("N/A")`, so no registry or other infrastructure is needed; because the transport is
real rather than `injvm://`, values are genuinely serialized.

`build.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.20"
    application
}
repositories { mavenCentral() }
dependencies {
    implementation("org.apache.dubbo:dubbo:3.3.6")
    implementation("io.netty:netty-all:4.1.118.Final")
    implementation("org.javassist:javassist:3.30.2-GA")
    implementation("org.slf4j:slf4j-simple:2.0.13")
}
kotlin { jvmToolchain(21) }
application { mainClass = "repro.MainKt" }
```

`src/main/java/repro/JReply.java` and `JFound.java` — a Java 17 sealed hierarchy, to show this is
not Kotlin-specific:

```java
package repro;

import java.io.Serializable;

public sealed interface JReply extends Serializable permits JFound {}
```

```java
package repro;

public final class JFound implements JReply {
    private String text;

    public JFound() {}

    public JFound(String text) {
        this.text = text;
    }

    public String getText() {
        return text;
    }

    public void setText(String text) {
        this.text = text;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "JFound(" + text + ")";
    }
}
```

`src/main/kotlin/Main.kt`:

```kotlin
package repro

import java.io.Serializable
import org.apache.dubbo.config.*
import org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap

sealed interface Reply : Serializable

data class Found(val text: String) : Reply

data object NotFound : Reply

interface ReplyService {
    fun lookup(key: String): Reply       // returns Found or NotFound
    fun javaLookup(key: String): JReply  // Java 17 sealed, same shape
}

class ReplyServiceImpl : ReplyService {
    override fun lookup(key: String): Reply = if (key == "x") Found("hit") else NotFound
    override fun javaLookup(key: String): JReply = JFound("hit")
}

private fun attempt(label: String, call: () -> Any) {
    try {
        println("$label -> OK: ${call()}")
    } catch (t: Throwable) {
        val root = generateSequence(t) { it.cause }.last()
        println("$label -> ${root::class.java.name}: ${root.message?.lines()?.first()}")
    }
}

fun main() {
    DubboBootstrap.getInstance()
        .application(ApplicationConfig("sealed-repro"))
        .registry(RegistryConfig("N/A"))
        .protocol(ProtocolConfig("dubbo", 20883))
        .service(ServiceConfig<ReplyService>().apply {
            setInterface(ReplyService::class.java)
            setRef(ReplyServiceImpl())
        })
        .start()

    val svc = ReferenceConfig<ReplyService>().apply {
        setInterface(ReplyService::class.java)
        url = "dubbo://127.0.0.1:20883"
    }.get()

    println("Dubbo ${org.apache.dubbo.common.Version.getVersion()}, no security/serialize.allowlist supplied")
    attempt("kotlin data class  (subtype of sealed Reply) ") { svc.lookup("x") }
    attempt("kotlin data object (subtype of sealed Reply) ") { svc.lookup("y") }
    attempt("java 17 sealed     (subtype of sealed JReply)") { svc.javaLookup("x") }

    DubboBootstrap.getInstance().destroy()
}
```

`gradle run` prints (long lines wrapped, otherwise verbatim):

```
Dubbo 3.3.6, no security/serialize.allowlist supplied
kotlin data class  (subtype of sealed Reply)  -> org.apache.dubbo.remoting.RemotingException:
  Failed to send response: ... result=AppResponse [value=Found(text=hit), exception=null]],
  cause: java.io.IOException: org.apache.dubbo.common.serialize.SerializationException:
  java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: [Serialization Security] Serialized class repro.Found is
  not in allow list. Current mode is `STRICT`, will disallow to deserialize it by default.
  Please add it into security/serialize.allowlist or follow FAQ to configure it.
kotlin data object (subtype of sealed Reply)  -> ... Serialized class repro.NotFound is not in allow list ...
java 17 sealed     (subtype of sealed JReply) -> ... Serialized class repro.JFound is not in allow list ...
```

`Reply`, `JReply` and `ReplyService` are all in the allow list. `Found`, `NotFound` and `JFound` are
not. Note that the check fires while the **provider serializes the response**, so the consumer sees
a `RemotingException` wrapping the `IllegalArgumentException` rather than a deserialization failure.

A larger demo exists that sends one payload down each route by which auto-trust can reach a class,
with Java controls, so the pattern is isolated rather than inferred:

```
route to payload           | declared as    | gate hit
---------------------------+----------------+--------------
direct param/return        | DirectPlain    | SERIALIZABLE   (not Serializable; a Java POJO behaves the same)
direct param/return        | DirectSerial.  | --             (trusted)
field of param/return      | Envelope       | --             (trusted)
generic type argument      | List<Listed>   | --             (trusted)
subtype of sealed          | Reply          | ALLOWLIST      <-- this report (Kotlin data class)
subtype of sealed          | Reply          | ALLOWLIST      <-- this report (Kotlin data object)
subtype of sealed          | JSealedReply   | ALLOWLIST      <-- this report (Java 17 sealed)
subtype of interface       | JReply (Java)  | ALLOWLIST      (non-sealed: cannot be enumerated)
```

Only the subtype route fails. Direct, field and generic routes all pass, and nothing about Kotlin or
`data class` varies between those rows.


### What you expected to happen

The subtypes a sealed type permits should be auto-trusted along with the parent.

A sealed type enumerates its subtypes in its own source, and the JVM refuses to load any subtype
absent from that list. Trusting them therefore grants exactly the set the author declared and
nothing an attacker can extend — a more precise grant than the package-prefix trust Dubbo already
applies when `trustSerializeClassLevel` is set. A non-sealed hierarchy is open, cannot be
enumerated, and must keep behaving as it does today.

What happens instead is that the developer has to list every subtype by hand, repeat that for every
sealed hierarchy, and remember to update it whenever a subtype is added — for a set the compiler
already knows in full.

- [x] I am sure that all the content I provide is in English.


### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/dubbo/issues?q=is%3Aissue) and found no similar issues.


### Apache Dubbo Component

Java SDK (apache/dubbo)

### Dubbo Version

Dubbo Java 3.3.6, OpenJDK 21 (Amazon Corretto 21.0.5), macOS 15.6 (OS-independent)


### Steps to reproduce this issue


`ServiceConfigBase.checkRef` reports a service whose `ref` does not implement the declared
interface. Its message is built by `getClassDesc`, which dereferences `Class#getClassLoader()`:

```java
private String getClassDesc(Class clazz) {
    ClassLoader classLoader = clazz.getClassLoader();
    return clazz.getName() + "[classloader=" + classLoader.getClass().getName() + "@"
            + classLoader.hashCode() + "]";
}
```

`Class#getClassLoader()` returns **null for any bootstrap-loaded class**, i.e. every JDK type. So
when a JDK type is on either side of the mismatch, the check throws `NullPointerException` from
inside its own diagnostic and the real misconfiguration is never reported.

Export a service whose declared interface is a JDK type that the ref does not implement. This is a
complete `main`, with a `dubbo` dependency and nothing else — no registry or other infrastructure:

```java
import org.apache.dubbo.config.ApplicationConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.ProtocolConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.RegistryConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap;

public class JavaRepro {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ServiceConfig<Object> service = new ServiceConfig<>();
        service.setInterface(Runnable.class); // GreeterServiceImpl does not implement Runnable
        service.setRef(new GreeterServiceImpl());

        DubboBootstrap.newInstance()
                .application(new ApplicationConfig("java-repro"))
                .registry(new RegistryConfig("N/A"))
                .protocol(new ProtocolConfig("dubbo", 20896))
                .service(service)
                .start();
    }
}
```

Result on 3.3.6:

```
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "Object.getClass()" because "classLoader" is null
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfigBase.getClassDesc(ServiceConfigBase.java:162)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfigBase.checkRef(ServiceConfigBase.java:156)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig.checkAndUpdateSubConfigs(ServiceConfig.java:508)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig.postProcessRefresh(ServiceConfig.java:549)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.AbstractConfig.refresh(AbstractConfig.java:734)
    ...
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap.start(DubboBootstrap.java:219)
```

Note it surfaces during application start, several frames from the config that caused it, with
nothing naming the service or the interface.

Substituting a **user-defined** wrong interface reports correctly, because its loader is non-null:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: The class ergo.GreeterServiceImpl[classloader=jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@746933701]
unimplemented interface ergo.UnrelatedService[classloader=jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@746933701]!
```

That contrast is what narrows the bug to a JDK type being on either side.


### What you expected to happen

`checkRef` should report the misconfiguration it was written to report, regardless of which loader
the classes came from:

```
The class ergo.GreeterServiceImpl[classloader=jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@746933701]
unimplemented interface java.lang.Runnable[classloader=bootstrap]!
```

That is what a local build of the fix produces for the same `main`.


### Anything else

I kinda added new term `bootstrap` to the API, so user may be surprised by that. I think if you have a better name, it could be replaced (I was about `no-classloader` or just `default`)

### Dubbo Version

### Steps to reproduce this issue


`ServiceConfigBase.checkRef` reports a service whose `ref` does not implement the declared
interface. Its message is built by `getClassDesc`, which dereferences `Class#getClassLoader()`:

```java
private String getClassDesc(Class clazz) {
    ClassLoader classLoader = clazz.getClassLoader();
    return clazz.getName() + "[classloader=" + classLoader.getClass().getName() + "@"
            + classLoader.hashCode() + "]";
}
```

`Class#getClassLoader()` returns **null for any bootstrap-loaded class**, i.e. every JDK type. So
when a JDK type is on either side of the mismatch, the check throws `NullPointerException` from
inside its own diagnostic and the real misconfiguration is never reported.

Export a service whose declared interface is a JDK type that the ref does not implement. This is a
complete `main`, with a `dubbo` dependency and nothing else — no registry or other infrastructure:

```java
import org.apache.dubbo.config.ApplicationConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.ProtocolConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.RegistryConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig;
import org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap;

public class JavaRepro {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ServiceConfig<Object> service = new ServiceConfig<>();
        service.setInterface(Runnable.class); // GreeterServiceImpl does not implement Runnable
        service.setRef(new GreeterServiceImpl());

        DubboBootstrap.newInstance()
                .application(new ApplicationConfig("java-repro"))
                .registry(new RegistryConfig("N/A"))
                .protocol(new ProtocolConfig("dubbo", 20896))
                .service(service)
                .start();
    }
}
```

Result on 3.3.6:

```
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "Object.getClass()" because "classLoader" is null
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfigBase.getClassDesc(ServiceConfigBase.java:162)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfigBase.checkRef(ServiceConfigBase.java:156)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig.checkAndUpdateSubConfigs(ServiceConfig.java:508)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig.postProcessRefresh(ServiceConfig.java:549)
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.AbstractConfig.refresh(AbstractConfig.java:734)
    ...
    at org.apache.dubbo.config.bootstrap.DubboBootstrap.start(DubboBootstrap.java:219)
```

Note it surfaces during application start, several frames from the config that caused it, with
nothing naming the service or the interface.

Substituting a **user-defined** wrong interface reports correctly, because its loader is non-null:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: The class ergo.GreeterServiceImpl[classloader=jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@746933701]
unimplemented interface ergo.UnrelatedService[classloader=jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@746933701]!
```

That contrast is what narrows the bug to a JDK type being on either side.


### What you expected to happen

`checkRef` should report the misconfiguration it was written to report, regardless of which loader
the classes came from:

```
The class ergo.GreeterServiceImpl[classloader=jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@746933701]
unimplemented interface java.lang.Runnable[classloader=bootstrap]!
```

That is what a local build of the fix produces for the same `main`.


### Anything else

I kinda added new term `bootstrap` to the API, so user may be surprised by that. I think if you have a better name, it could be replaced (I was about `no-classloader` or just `default`)

### Pre-check

- [x] I am sure that all the content I provide is in English.


### Search before asking

- [x] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/dubbo/issues?q=is%3Aissue) and found no similar issues.


### Apache Dubbo Component

Java SDK (apache/dubbo)

### Dubbo Version

Apache Dubbo source: 3.3.7-SNAPSHOT, branch `3.3`, commit `ae809de2fc81b408194240965eb20bf27e6971df`.
Windows, OpenJDK 21, Maven 3.6.3.

Verification used an isolated Maven/JUnit harness: eight relevant implementation/interface files were copied byte-for-byte from this commit, with released Dubbo 3.3.6 artifacts supplying supporting dependencies. The paths under review were compiled from the current source, not taken from those dependency jars. This is not a full current-branch reactor build or a networked RPC deployment.

### Steps to reproduce this issue

After a key has been promoted into the main cache by two puts, a subsequent put for the same key does not update its value. The third put only records the key in the history/pre-cache, while the main cache keeps the earlier value.

Minimal JUnit Jupiter regression:

```java
import org.apache.dubbo.common.utils.LRU2Cache;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

class LRU2UpdateTest {
    @Test void promotedKeyMustAcceptUpdates() {
        LRU2Cache<String, String> cache = new LRU2Cache<>(10);
        cache.put("key", "v1"); // history
        cache.put("key", "v1"); // promotion
        assertEquals("v1", cache.get("key"));

        cache.put("key", "v2"); // update existing key
        assertEquals("v2", cache.get("key")); // FAILS: v1
    }
}
```

The same result was reproduced through the current `org.apache.dubbo.cache.support.lru.LruCache` implementation:

```java
LruCache cache = new LruCache(
    URL.valueOf("dubbo://127.0.0.1:20880/example.Service?cache.size=10"));
cache.put("key", "v1");
cache.put("key", "v1");
cache.put("key", "v2");
assertEquals("v2", cache.get("key")); // FAILS: v1
```

No concurrency, registry, or remote service is needed.

### What you expected to happen

`put` must update an entry that is already in the main cache; the two-touch admission policy for a new key should not discard an update to an admitted key.

Actual output from both regressions:

```text
LRU2 after update: v1
LruCache plugin after update: v1
expected: <v2> but was: <v1>
```

### Anything else

Root cause: [`LRU2Cache.put`](https://github.com/apache/dubbo/blob/ae809de2fc81b408194240965eb20bf27e6971df/dubbo-common/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/common/utils/LRU2Cache.java) checks only `preCache.containsKey(key)`. Promotion removes the key from `preCache`; an update therefore enters the history-only branch even though `super.containsKey(key)` is true. The cache plugin delegates writes directly to this method.

A possible fix is to handle keys already in the main cache before applying new-key admission. Add a regression for the third write after promotion.

Searched LRU2Cache and LRU update-related issues/PRs. #16170 concerns `computeIfAbsent` concurrency and #16038/#16053 concern capacity reduction; this report concerns deterministic, single-threaded `put` updates and is independent of those changes.

Root cause: [`LRU2Cache.put`](https://github.com/apache/dubbo/blob/ae809de2fc81b408194240965eb20bf27e6971df/dubbo-common/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/common/utils/LRU2Cache.java) checks only `preCache.containsKey(key)`. Promotion removes the key from `preCache`; an update therefore enters the history-only branch even though `super.containsKey(key)` is true. The cache plugin delegates writes directly to this method.

A possible fix is to handle keys already in the main cache before applying new-key admission. Add a regression for the third write after promotion.

Searched LRU2Cache and LRU update-related issues/PRs. #16170 concerns `computeIfAbsent` concurrency and #16038/#16053 concern capacity reduction; this report concerns deterministic, single-threaded `put` updates and is independent of those changes.
