### Bug Description

**What happened:**

With the column stats index enabled, a `LIKE 'abc%'` (or `startswith`) filter prunes a file whose values all start with the prefix, so the query silently returns too few rows. `DataSkippingUtils` translates the filter into `name_minValue <= 'abc' AND 'abc' <= name_maxValue`, but values starting with a prefix sort after the prefix itself (`'abc123' > 'abc'`), so a file whose min value is `'abc123'` fails the check. The partition stats index goes through the same translation.

**What you expected:**

Both rows returned.

**Steps to reproduce:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INT, name STRING) USING hudi
TBLPROPERTIES (primaryKey = 'id', 'hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable' = 'true');

INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'abc123'), (2, 'abc345');

SELECT id FROM t WHERE name LIKE 'abc%' ORDER BY id;
-- expected: 1, 2
-- actual: no rows
```

### Environment

**Hudi version:** master (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT)
**Query engine:** Spark 3.5
**Relevant configs:** `hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable=true`, `hoodie.enable.data.skipping=true` (default)

body_text:
### Task Description

Add an optional, persistent Spark Connect endpoint under `hudi-lakehouse`, following the direction in [discussion #19843](https://github.com/apache/hudi/discussions/19843). The endpoint will serve Hudi reads and writes through ADBC clients and be shared by the agent gateway, Superset, and Zeppelin.

### Scope

- Provide a Hudi-enabled Spark Connect image with pinned, compatible Spark/Hudi/Scala/Java versions and required dependencies.
- Add a `hudi-spark-connect` Helm chart with catalog, object storage, existing Secret, resource, and service configuration. Default to cluster-internal access.
- Integrate with the local-dev quickstart without breaking the existing Trino and Spark writer paths.
- Install ADBC dependencies on clients; the server runs Spark Connect, not a separate ADBC service.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The image builds reproducibly and the chart passes Helm lint/template checks.
- [ ] A clean local Kubernetes environment can deploy the endpoint against the local-dev catalog and object store.
- [ ] A Foundry ADBC client can create a Hudi table and execute SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, with readback assertions.
- [ ] Tables remain accessible after an endpoint restart.
- [ ] Startup, connection, and teardown instructions are included.

Gateway write tools are out of scope; endpoint write access is for direct clients.

### Task Type

Other — runtime packaging and deployment.

body_text:
### Task Description

Connect `hudi-agent-gateway`, Superset, and Zeppelin to the Spark Connect endpoint through Foundry ADBC. Prioritize gateway integration, then package the BI examples. Background: [discussion #19843](https://github.com/apache/hudi/discussions/19843).

### Scope

- Add an ADBC-backed Spark Connect client to the gateway, including Spark SQL and metadata handling, bounded result fetching, connection cleanup, and timeout/cancellation handling with clearly documented limitations.
- Preserve `list_tables`, `describe_table`, and `query_lakehouse` interfaces and SELECT-only guardrails. Gateway write tools remain out of scope.
- Update gateway dependencies, connection settings, readiness checks, and Helm values. Install the ADBC Driver Manager and Foundry driver in the client runtime.
- Package the Superset SQLAlchemy adapter with pinned dependencies, SQL Lab instructions, and a dashboard example. Support direct DML with Allow DML enabled and handle statements without result sets.
- Provide a Zeppelin `%python` notebook using ADBC for queries, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, and result rendering; this is not native `%jdbc` support.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Gateway table discovery, table descriptions, and Agent/MCP queries work against the Helm-deployed endpoint.
- [ ] Gateway rejects write statements and preserves existing read-only behavior.
- [ ] Superset and Zeppelin can query, execute INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, and read back the changes through ADBC.
- [ ] Examples include reproducible dependency and connection setup without modifying upstream driver binaries.

### Task Type

Other — client integration and examples.

### Related Issues

Depends on #20231 for the Helm-deployed endpoint.

### Review follow-ups from #20243 (2026-10-22)

The latest local Gateway implementation uses the official PySpark Connect client; ADBC remains the direct BI-client path. The original ADBC-only Gateway plan above is superseded by this implementation choice. The local three-turn Chat UI query flow passed, but this is not completion of all acceptance criteria.

- [ ] Propagate Chat UI Stop through the agent/tool task to Spark and add a regression test. In the local run, the UI stopped but the Spark job was still running 24 seconds later; direct Gateway timeout/cancellation did stop Spark jobs. Verify session-scoped cancellation and that later queries remain usable.
- [ ] Preserve timestamp timezone semantics and nested struct field names in Gateway JSON results. Local output omitted timezone information and represented structs as arrays; verify decimal precision and result truncation alongside the fix.
- [ ] Keep the initial Superset SQLAlchemy adapter and tested examples under `hudi-lakehouse`; evaluate upstreaming separately.
- [ ] Document client-specific cancellation limits. Foundry ADBC 0.2.1 `adbc_cancel()` returned a cancellation error to the client, but server-side write cancellation/rollback was not established.

Gateway remains SELECT-only. Direct-client failure/retry and broader endpoint validation are tracked in #20233. These items are follow-up work, not fixes already included in #20243.

### Task Description

Add repeatable end-to-end validation and a complete quickstart for the Helm-deployed Spark Connect endpoint and its gateway/BI clients. Turn the local experiments from [discussion #19843](https://github.com/apache/hudi/discussions/19843) into reproducible checks.

### Scope

- Validate Agent/MCP → hudi-agent-gateway → ADBC → Spark Connect → Hudi, including table discovery, descriptions, query results, and rejection of writes by gateway guardrails.
- Validate Superset SQL Lab queries and direct DML, dashboard refresh after writes, and Zeppelin notebook query/write result rendering.
- Add direct-client checks for table creation, filtering, aggregation, date grouping, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, MERGE INTO, read-after-write, and visibility of commits from an independent writer.
- Use isolated test data, assert results after each mutation, and provide cleanup and clear pass/fail output.
- Document the complete setup, tested server/client versions, required adapters, known limitations, troubleshooting, and a small selection of query/result screenshots.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A clean local Kubernetes environment can follow the quickstart from deployment through all three client paths.
- [ ] Repeatable endpoint and gateway tests assert data correctness and read-only guardrails.
- [ ] Superset and Zeppelin application-level checks verify results and rendered output; any manual steps are explicit.
- [ ] Documentation distinguishes direct-client writes from the read-only gateway and verified behavior from untested functionality.
- [ ] Test data can be cleaned up without affecting unrelated tables.

Production-scale concurrency/isolation and broader JDBC compatibility are follow-up work, not claims established by these functional tests.

### Task Type

Test enhancement and documentation update.

### Related Issues

- #20231 — Helm-deployable Spark Connect endpoint.
- #20232 — Gateway and BI client integration.

Full end-to-end acceptance depends on both; endpoint tests can be developed alongside #20231.

### Review validation and operational follow-ups from #20243 (2026-10-22)

The latest local run used Spark 4.1.3 + Hudi 1.2.0, a Helm-deployed local[2] driver with a 2g heap/3Gi pod limit, Foundry ADBC 0.2.1, and the official PySpark Connect client for Gateway. Chat UI multi-turn queries and direct-client fault/result-size experiments ran; the complete matrix below remains open. Tracking these items does not imply reviewer approval to defer them from #20243.

#### SQL and external-writer validation

- [ ] Run the added live SQL matrix: MERGE, MoR snapshot/read-optimized reads and completed inline compaction, partitioned tables with HMS sync and Trino readback, CALL, time travel and incremental reads. Confirm server defaults create v8 tables without statement-level version pins.
- [ ] Run same-session freshness checks against an independent writer for commits, schema evolution and table recreation, first without refresh, then with explicit REFRESH TABLE if required. Record whether refresh is necessary.
- [ ] Validate Spark 3.5 and Flink external-writer combinations separately; the new fixture uses the same pinned Spark/Hudi image and does not establish cross-version compatibility.

The meeting narrowed required v1 delivery to interactive SQL reads/writes. General job submission and DataFrame-write integration are not required acceptance items.

#### Faults, result size and types

- [ ] Make disconnect, lost-response and driver-restart experiments repeatable with isolated tables. The local run observed a committed write after client disconnect; retrying INSERT after a lost response produced duplicates. Restart after a requested instant was followed by rollback and a successful write. Extend coverage to other partial-write phases and explicit cancellation; do not infer universal safe-retry or rollback guarantees. Concurrent-writer behavior was not covered.
- [ ] Run the requested million-row SELECT * case with the default 2g driver heap, recording row width, client/server memory, fetch mode and failure behavior. The completed first pass covered 10k/100k rows (~98 MiB payload at 100k), not millions. Foundry's 4 MiB gRPC receive limit rejected a ~10 MiB response; 1m Arrow batches allowed all tested ADBC reads to finish. Check wide individual rows too; batch size is not a total-result cap.
- [ ] Complete explicit TIMESTAMP_NTZ and _hoodie_* mapping checks. Decimal(38,18), timestamp microseconds and nested struct/array/map reads passed in the first run; verify timezone handling across client environments.
- [ ] Investigate the Hudi/Parquet write failure for arrays containing NULL elements. Direct SQL transport of a nullable array passed, so do not classify it as a Connect transport failure without further evidence.

Gateway Stop propagation and timestamp/struct JSON fixes are tracked in #20232.

#### Deployment and operations

- [ ] Validate the opt-in Kubernetes executor configuration: fixed worker count, driver/executor networking, RBAC, image availability and storage credentials. Validate dynamic allocation separately. The local[2] run does not establish distributed execution.
- [ ] Add SQL-aware readiness with separate catalog/storage checks. SELECT 1 alone does not verify HMS or S3 access.
- [ ] Add optional Spark UI access, event logs/history server, metrics and client-request-to-Spark-job/Hudi-commit correlation, with safe access controls.
- [ ] Add an opt-in kind live-CI job using allowlisted actions. Exercise deployment, SQL CRUD/MERGE, restart/readback and cleanup; clearly separate offline contract checks from live engine coverage.

These items are tracked follow-ups; production-scale concurrency/isolation and stronger recovery guarantees remain outside the claims of the current functional tests.

body_text:
When a table's `hoodie.properties` has no `hoodie.database.name` (for example, a table written through the Spark datasource without that option and registered in a catalog later), `HoodieFileIndex.getConfigProperties` guesses the database from the session's current database and calls `spark.catalog.tableExists(guessedDb, tableName)` to merge catalog table properties.

That merge is best-effort, but the catalog call is not guarded. With a session catalog whose `tableExists` throws for the guessed identifier (for example, a catalog that rejects the `default` database), a fully qualified read such as `SELECT * FROM db1.tbl` fails during planning, even though the query names the database and the table resolves. `USE db1` before the same query works, because the guess then happens to be right.

Expected: a failure to resolve a guessed database should not fail the read; the catalog properties merge should be skipped with a warning. When the database is recorded in `hoodie.properties`, behaviour should stay as it is.

body_text:
On the Hudi Streamer path without a transformer, `LazyCastingIterator` calls `HoodieAvroUtils.rewriteRecordDeep(record, targetSchema)` for every source record. The target schema is parsed per partition, so it is never the same instance as the record schema, and every record pays a deep Avro `Schema.equals` before being returned unchanged. On a 30-column schema that is about 0.8 us and 4.9 KB of allocation per record.

Proposal: compare each distinct source schema instance with the target once, and return records of an equal schema as is.

body_text:
Bulk insert through the row writer (the default for bulk_insert) ignores `hoodie.parquet.bloom.filter.enabled=false` and always writes the parquet footer bloom filter. `HoodieInternalRowFileWriterFactory` checks only whether meta fields are populated, while the Avro, Spark and Flink writer factories use the shared `HoodieFileWriterFactory.enableBloomFilter` added with the config in #10457. With default settings the bloom adds about 430 KB to every base file footer, which every reader loads and parses.

Proposal: have the row-writer factory call the shared `enableBloomFilter` / `createBloomFilter`.

Prepped Spark writes on the default AVRO record type (Spark SQL `UPDATE`, pk-less `MERGE INTO`, datasource prepped upserts) call `HoodieSchemaUtils.removeMetadataFields(dataFileSchema)` inside the per-record loop of `HoodieCreateRecordUtils.createHoodieRecordRdd`, building a new Avro schema for every record; each field copy also re-parses the Avro version string (`HoodieAvroUtils.gteqAvro1_12`). Proposal: build the schema once per partition and evaluate the Avro version checks once.

body_text:
With an expression index on a function of a column, data skipping also uses that index for filters on a different function of the same column. Example: with `create index idx on t using column_stats(city) options(expr='lower')`, the query `select * from t where upper(city) = 'CITY_4242'` returns no rows (1,224 with `hoodie.enable.data.skipping=false`), and `where length(city) = 9` fails with `ClassCastException: String cannot be cast to Integer`.

Cause: `ExpressionIndexSupport.extractQueryAndLiterals` unwraps any `UnaryExpression` over the index's source column without checking that it is the index's function. Proposal: match the filter's function against the index definition before using the index, and fall back to column stats otherwise.

### Task Description

**What needs to be done:**

On object storage every file-system call (HEAD, GET, LIST, PUT) is a round trip, and every executor request to the
embedded timeline server is a driver round trip served under a lock. Small redundant costs per file, file group, task,
partition or instant add up to the dominant latency on large tables, and they are invisible in tests that use a
handful of files on one thread.

An audit of master instrumented every storage call (and every executor to timeline-server request) made by Spark
writes, table services, queries, SQL DMLs and HoodieStreamer, across COW and MOR, table versions 6, 8 and current, the
metadata table on and off, the timeline server on and off, the index types and the write handles. It found redundant
calls such as: metadata-table HFiles opened and downloaded three times per read, base-file footers read twice and
status-checked twice per file, column stats re-reading every new file's footer, executor tasks rebuilding metadata
readers and file-system views, per-task timeline-server lookups the driver could answer once, and a per-request
lock plus timeline hash in the timeline server. It also surfaced several correctness bugs.

This issue tracks the fixes. Each sub-issue describes one problem with its evidence; each PR carries a test that
counts the calls (or reproduces the bug) so the regression class is guarded.

**Why this task is needed:**

On object storage each redundant call is a 10-100 ms round trip, and the costs found grow with files, file groups, tasks, partitions or instants, so they dominate latency on large tables.

### Task Type

Performance optimization

### Related Issues

**Parent feature issue:** (none)
**Related issues:**


- #20258 (PR #20259): metadata table HFile log files read once instead of three times

- #20260 (PR #20261): MOR records silently dropped when the operation metadata field is enabled (bug)

- #20262 (PR #20263): bloom index key check reuses driver-resolved base files instead of timeline-server lookups

- #20264 (PR #20265): timeline server checks view freshness without the per-table view lock

- #20266 (PR #20267): data skipping returned too few rows on METADATA_ONLY bootstrap tables with column stats (bug)

### Task Description

**What needs to be done:**
On table version 10 the metadata table writes native HFile log files. Every read of one of these files opens it 3 times and downloads the whole file 3 times: once for the footer (block header), once when the reader loads its schema and meta info, and once for the record or key iterator. It also makes 2 file status calls when the log file size is known from the listing, and 4 when it is not (MDT compaction builds log files from the plan's file names). Each read should download the file once per reader and reuse the length the file slice listing already returned.

**Why this task is needed:**
This cost applies to every metadata table read path that touches log files: writer index lookups, column stats and partition stats updates, data skipping on the driver, the timeline server and MDT compaction. It scales with lookups x log files, not with the number of keys, and on object storage every extra open and status call is a round trip. In a local Spark harness (COW table, version 10, SIMPLE index, column stats + partition stats, 9 writes + 12 reads), calls on metadata table data files totalled 2045 opens, 1336 file status calls and 21.6 MB read. In one upsert, 8 executor tasks reading 6 `column_stats` log files made 144 opens and 98 status calls.

### Task Type

Performance optimization

### Related Issues

**Parent feature issue:** #20257

**Related issues:** #18419 (HFile block cache)


**Fixed by:** #20259

### Bug Description

**What happened:**
On a MOR table (table versions 6, 8 and 10) with `hoodie.allow.operation.metadata.field=true`, upserts and deletes through the Spark datasource, Spark SQL or the Java client lose every record routed to a log file, and the write still reports success. These writers do not set a `HoodieOperation` on their records, but `HoodieAppendHandle.populateMetadataFields` calls `hoodieRecord.getOperation().getName()` whenever the flag is on, so every record fails with a `NullPointerException`. With `hoodie.write.ignore.failed` at its default `true`, the failure is only recorded on the handle's write status, and `close()` drops that status when no log block was appended. The deltacommit completes without the records, and the next compaction finds no log files. Flink is not affected because it always sets the operation.

**What you expected:**
The upsert lands in the log file and is visible in snapshot reads, or the write fails.

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. In spark-shell, write two rows to a new MOR table with the operation field enabled:
   ```scala
   val opts = Map(
     "hoodie.table.name" -> "t",
     "hoodie.datasource.write.table.type" -> "MERGE_ON_READ",
     "hoodie.datasource.write.operation" -> "upsert",
     "hoodie.datasource.write.recordkey.field" -> "id",
     "hoodie.datasource.write.partitionpath.field" -> "part",
     "hoodie.table.ordering.fields" -> "ts",
     "hoodie.allow.operation.metadata.field" -> "true")
   Seq(("1", "a", 1L, "p1"), ("2", "b", 1L, "p1")).toDF("id", "name", "ts", "part")
     .write.format("hudi").options(opts).mode("overwrite").save(path)
   ```
2. Upsert one of them: `Seq(("1", "a2", 2L, "p1")).toDF("id", "name", "ts", "part").write.format("hudi").options(opts).mode("append").save(path)`. The write succeeds.
3. Read it back: `spark.read.format("hudi").load(path).select("id", "name").show()` returns `1:a, 2:b` instead of `1:a2, 2:b`. With `hoodie.allow.operation.metadata.field=false` it returns `1:a2, 2:b`.

### Environment

**Hudi version:** master (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT); the null dereference exists since 0.9.0
**Query engine:** Spark 3.5 (also the Java client)
**Relevant configs:** `hoodie.allow.operation.metadata.field=true`, `hoodie.write.ignore.failed=true` (default), MOR table, table versions 6, 8 and 10

### Logs and Stack Trace

```
ERROR HoodieAppendHandle: Error writing record ...
java.lang.NullPointerException
	at org.apache.hudi.io.HoodieAppendHandle.populateMetadataFields(HoodieAppendHandle.java:453)
```

**Fixed by:** #20261

body_text:
### Task Description

**What needs to be done:**
Let the bloom index key-check stage use the base files the driver already resolved while loading key ranges, instead of looking each one up again on the executors, and let the BLOOM and SIMPLE index footer and key reads open parquet base files from their known size instead of looking up the file status first.

**Why this task is needed:**
The key check builds a `HoodieKeyLookupHandle` per candidate file group, and the handle resolves the latest base file through the file system view twice (once for the bloom filter, once in `getLookupResult`). On executors that is the remote timeline-server view, so every (task, candidate base file) costs two `getLatestBaseFile` requests, each a per-partition scan under the view read lock, for every BLOOM / GLOBAL_BLOOM upsert or delete with the timeline server on (both defaults). The count grows linearly with file groups per partition. Each parquet open also stats the file first (a HEAD on object storage) although its size is already known from the listing or the metadata table.

On a local Spark COW upsert harness, going from 1 to 4 file groups per partition grows executor timeline-server requests from `HoodieBloomIndexCheckFunction` from 64 to 256 (driver requests stay flat), and executor base-file `getFileStatus` calls from 152 to 352.

The two lookups per handle date from #726 (0.5.0) and became timeline-server requests when the embedded timeline server became the default (#1634, 0.5.3). #6793 (HUDI-4917, 0.13.0) already reuses the driver-resolved base file in the range-info stage, but not in the key check.

### Task Type

Performance optimization

### Related Issues

**Parent feature issue:** #20257

**Related issues:**
- #6793 (driver-resolved base file for the range-info stage)


**Fixed by:** #20263

**What needs to be done:**
Let the bloom index key-check stage use the base files the driver already resolved while loading key ranges, instead of looking each one up again on the executors, and let the BLOOM and SIMPLE index footer and key reads open parquet base files from their known size instead of looking up the file status first.

**Why this task is needed:**
The key check builds a `HoodieKeyLookupHandle` per candidate file group, and the handle resolves the latest base file through the file system view twice (once for the bloom filter, once in `getLookupResult`). On executors that is the remote timeline-server view, so every (task, candidate base file) costs two `getLatestBaseFile` requests, each a per-partition scan under the view read lock, for every BLOOM / GLOBAL_BLOOM upsert or delete with the timeline server on (both defaults). The count grows linearly with file groups per partition. Each parquet open also stats the file first (a HEAD on object storage) although its size is already known from the listing or the metadata table.

On a local Spark COW upsert harness, going from 1 to 4 file groups per partition grows executor timeline-server requests from `HoodieBloomIndexCheckFunction` from 64 to 256 (driver requests stay flat), and executor base-file `getFileStatus` calls from 152 to 352.

The two lookups per handle date from #726 (0.5.0) and became timeline-server requests when the embedded timeline server became the default (#1634, 0.5.3). #6793 (HUDI-4917, 0.13.0) already reuses the driver-resolved base file in the range-info stage, but not in the key check.

Performance optimization

body_text:
### Task Description

**What needs to be done:**
Check whether the timeline server view is behind the client without taking the per-table view lock and without rebuilding and hashing the view timeline on every request. Today every file system view request (with the default refresh check on) enters `synchronized (view)` unconditionally and builds a filtered copy of the view timeline (`filterCompletedOrMajorOrMinorCompactionInstants`), whose constructor SHA-256 hashes every instant; the same filter and hash run again after the handler. Between two syncs of the server view that filtered timeline and its hash never change, so the work can be done once per view timeline, and requests from clients that are already in sync do not need the lock. The fix must keep the guarantee from #8079 that a request is never answered from a half-synced view.

**Why this task is needed:**
Each request costs two O(active instants) hashes, and all requests for one table queue on one monitor while hashing, even when nothing needs to be refreshed. Requests per commit scale with tasks and partitions (index and small-file lookups, base-file lookups in update tasks, clean and clustering planners), so large tables with wide stages serialize on this lock. 64 concurrent up-to-date requests filter and hash the view timeline 128 times, an up-to-date request blocks while another thread holds the view monitor, and a local micro-benchmark (mocked view, 32 client threads, 2000 active instants, on a heavily loaded laptop) tops out around 1400 req/s with p50 17 ms, and around 740 req/s when the timeline ends in a clean (the trailing-clean check hashes the timeline once more under the lock).

### Task Type

Performance optimization

### Related Issues

**Parent feature issue:** #20257

**Related issues:** #8079 (moved the check under the unconditional lock), #19946 (trailing-clean refresh exemption in the same check), #20239 (open, same method)


**Fixed by:** #20265

body_text:
### Bug Description

**What happened:**

After a METADATA_ONLY bootstrap, a Spark snapshot query that filters on a data column silently returns too few rows (often zero) once the column stats index is enabled on the table. That happens on the first later write with Spark's defaults (column stats and partition stats on), and data skipping is on by default, so no special setting is needed.

The column stats of a bootstrapped file group come from its skeleton file, which only has the Hudi meta columns. Partition stats pruning keeps only partitions with a matching stats row, so a fully bootstrapped partition is pruned and a partition with bootstrapped and rewritten file groups is pruned by the rewritten files' value range alone. Column stats pruning keeps a file with no stats only if it has no record for any filtered column, so a filter that also references a meta column (`_hoodie_record_key = 'trip_7' and rider = 'rider_7'`) prunes the skeleton file. Flink's `FileStatsIndex` and `PartitionStatsIndex` likely have the same gap (not verified).

**What you expected:**

The same rows with data skipping on and off.

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Write a partitioned parquet dataset (`_row_key`, `rider`, `driver`, `timestamp`, `datestr`, ...) to `srcPath`.
2. Bootstrap it in METADATA_ONLY mode (the default selector) with `hoodie.datasource.write.operation=bootstrap`, `hoodie.bootstrap.base.path=srcPath`, record key `_row_key`, partition path `datestr`, and `hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable=false`.
3. Upsert a few rows with the Spark defaults, which builds column stats and partition stats over the skeleton files.
4. Compare `spark.read.format("hudi").load(basePath).filter("driver >= 'driver_5'").count()` with the same query and `hoodie.enable.data.skipping=false`: 18 vs 56 rows.
5. With partition stats disabled, single data-column filters are correct, but `_hoodie_commit_time = '00000000000001' and driver >= 'driver_5'` returns 1 row instead of 55. COW and MOR behave the same.

### Environment

**Hudi version:** master (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT); reachable by default since 1.0.1
**Query engine:** Spark 3.5
**Relevant configs:** `hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable=true`, `hoodie.metadata.index.partition.stats.enable=true`, `hoodie.enable.data.skipping=true` (all defaults), METADATA_ONLY bootstrap

### Logs and Stack Trace

_No response_

**Parent issue:** #20257


**Fixed by:** #20267

**What happened:**

After a METADATA_ONLY bootstrap, a Spark snapshot query that filters on a data column silently returns too few rows (often zero) once the column stats index is enabled on the table. That happens on the first later write with Spark's defaults (column stats and partition stats on), and data skipping is on by default, so no special setting is needed.

The column stats of a bootstrapped file group come from its skeleton file, which only has the Hudi meta columns. Partition stats pruning keeps only partitions with a matching stats row, so a fully bootstrapped partition is pruned and a partition with bootstrapped and rewritten file groups is pruned by the rewritten files' value range alone. Column stats pruning keeps a file with no stats only if it has no record for any filtered column, so a filter that also references a meta column (`_hoodie_record_key = 'trip_7' and rider = 'rider_7'`) prunes the skeleton file. Flink's `FileStatsIndex` and `PartitionStatsIndex` likely have the same gap (not verified).

**What you expected:**

The same rows with data skipping on and off.

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Write a partitioned parquet dataset (`_row_key`, `rider`, `driver`, `timestamp`, `datestr`, ...) to `srcPath`.
2. Bootstrap it in METADATA_ONLY mode (the default selector) with `hoodie.datasource.write.operation=bootstrap`, `hoodie.bootstrap.base.path=srcPath`, record key `_row_key`, partition path `datestr`, and `hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable=false`.
3. Upsert a few rows with the Spark defaults, which builds column stats and partition stats over the skeleton files.
4. Compare `spark.read.format("hudi").load(basePath).filter("driver >= 'driver_5'").count()` with the same query and `hoodie.enable.data.skipping=false`: 18 vs 56 rows.
5. With partition stats disabled, single data-column filters are correct, but `_hoodie_commit_time = '00000000000001' and driver >= 'driver_5'` returns 1 row instead of 55. COW and MOR behave the same.

### Environment

**Hudi version:** master (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT); reachable by default since 1.0.1
**Query engine:** Spark 3.5
**Relevant configs:** `hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable=true`, `hoodie.metadata.index.partition.stats.enable=true`, `hoodie.enable.data.skipping=true` (all defaults), METADATA_ONLY bootstrap

body_text:
Reading or compacting MOR file groups that carry partial-update log records (from a partial `MERGE INTO`) spends most of the per-record merge cost comparing Avro schemas: 16% of executor CPU and 47% of allocation in a 6M-row Spark SQL run. `SparkRecordMergingUtils` builds the merged schema of a full-plus-partial merge by converting the Spark struct type back to a `HoodieSchema`, which drops field defaults, so the result is unequal to the reader schema but hashes the same. Every schema-keyed lookup holding both then compares the two field by field, once per merged record.

Proposal: reuse the reader schema as the merged schema when the merge covers every reader field.

When a 1.x writer creates a table with hoodie.write.table.version below 8, TableBuilder persists only hoodie.table.keygenerator.type, plus hoodie.table.keygenerator.class for USER_PROVIDED key generators. Hudi 0.x only knows hoodie.table.keygenerator.class, so it sees a table without a key generator and silently falls back to the write config, which can disagree with how the table was written.

The 8 to 7 downgrade handler already writes the class for exactly this reason. Table creation below version 8 should do the same.

### Task Description

## Summary

Track a focused improvement identified in #17128: support vectorized Parquet decoding for the base-file side of Spark MOR FileGroupReader (FGR), while retaining row-level merging and row output.

The broader read-performance audit already identifies this limitation, and its triage discussion recommends splitting independently actionable items. This issue scopes that item to the explicit non-vectorized base reader used by the MOR merge path. It is not a claim of a newly discovered regression, a duplicate of the session-configuration fixes, or a request for a fully columnar merge engine.

## Source observations

The following observations are pinned to upstream commit `be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e` (source inspection, not a benchmark of that commit), focusing on the Spark 3.4 implementation.

1. In [HoodieFileGroupReaderBasedFileFormat.scala, lines 274–283](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/HoodieFileGroupReaderBasedFileFormat.scala#L274-L283), the ordinary base reader uses `supportVectorizedRead`. However, when `isMOR && supportVectorizedRead`, the separate FGR base reader is constructed with `enableVectorizedRead = false`. The nearby comment attributes this to row-level merging and leaves a TODO for vectorized reader support.
2. The FGR branch [passes that reader into SparkFileFormatInternalRowReaderContext](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/HoodieFileGroupReaderBasedFileFormat.scala#L304-L307).
3. [HoodieMergeOnReadRDDV2.scala, lines 113–125](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/hudi/HoodieMergeOnReadRDDV2.scala#L113-L125) also constructs its Parquet FGR base reader with `vectorized = false`, separately from `OPTION_RETURNING_BATCH = false`.
4. [Spark34ParquetReader.scala, lines 167–229](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark3.4.x/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/Spark34ParquetReader.scala#L167-L229) has distinct vectorized-decoding and row-based ParquetRecordReader branches. Its [builder](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark3.4.x/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/Spark34ParquetReader.scala#L252-L295) passes the supplied `vectorized` argument into `enableVectorizedReader`; enabling Spark's vectorized-reader SQL setting alone does not override the explicit false in these FGR paths.

This concerns the reader supplied to FGR, not every MOR query or every base-file-only path. Likewise, `supportVectorizedRead: true` at the FileFormat level does not by itself demonstrate vectorized decoding inside FGR.

## Why investigate this?

For wide projections over base-plus-log file slices, column pruning eliminates little base-file work. Non-vectorized base decoding could therefore become a meaningful cost even if FGR improves other parts of the read path. This is a performance hypothesis, not evidence that the setting alone explains a cross-version regression. No isolated upstream before/after measurement is claimed here.

Vectorized decoding and returning ColumnarBatch to Spark are separate decisions. Could the base reader decode batches internally but expose compatible rows to the existing merge pipeline? This would not require vectorizing the merge algorithm itself. It is also not a proposal to simply flip the boolean without checking row representation, ownership and correctness.

## Proposed scope and validation

- Identify the constraints behind the current restriction: row representation (including UnsafeRow assumptions), batch-buffer reuse/lifetime, projection/schema evolution, and merge semantics.
- If feasible, support vectorized decoding for eligible Parquet base reads with row output, retaining a safe fallback for unsupported cases and covering both entry points above.
- Validate inserts, updates, partial updates, deletes, nulls, schema evolution and timestamp handling, including records retained across batch boundaries.
- Benchmark the current and candidate readers on the same upstream build baseline and frozen MOR snapshot, with identical resources and query expressions. Include narrow and full projections, base-plus-log slices, and base-only/log-only controls. Consume the projected values rather than relying on count(*) alone. Record scan/task time, input bytes, CPU/GC and spill, with repeated paired runs.

These are proposed validation steps, not completed results.

## Questions for maintainers

What correctness constraints must be addressed before vectorized base decoding can feed row-level FGR merging? In particular, which row-representation and buffer-lifetime contracts should an implementation preserve? If an existing implementation already covers this MOR-specific scope, please link it so this issue can be consolidated with that work.

### Task Type

Performance optimization

### Related Issues

- #17128 (HUDI-9674): umbrella Spark 1.X read-performance audit. It explicitly calls for exploring FGR vectorized reads; this issue proposes tracking that item separately.
- #20089 / PR #20090 and #20140 / PR #20193: related per-scan reader decisions and session-configuration mutation. Fixing those decisions is distinct from enabling vectorized decoding in the MOR-specific reader explicitly constructed with `false` at the pinned commit.
- #20182 / PR #20183: reports stale vectorization state and a `ColumnarBatchRow` / `UnsafeRow` mismatch, with a COW wide-nested-schema reproduction. Relevant to reader/output compatibility, but not evidence of the same failure in MOR merging.
- #17026 (HUDI-9443): reflection on `batchIdx` in the vectorized reader's per-row access. Relevant when considering a vectorized-decoding/row-output implementation; it does not itself address the MOR reader's explicit disablement.
- #20064: broader executor-overhead work in Hudi 1.x. Task serialization, configuration and schema work are separate performance factors, not attributed to vectorization by this issue.
- PR #13127 (HUDI-9302): related work enabling vectorized reading for file slices without log files; useful background for extending support to the MOR merge path.

In [HoodieFileGroupReaderBasedFileFormat.scala, lines 274–283](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/HoodieFileGroupReaderBasedFileFormat.scala#L274-L283), the ordinary base reader uses `supportVectorizedRead`. However, when `isMOR && supportVectorizedRead`, the separate FGR base reader is constructed with `enableVectorizedRead = false`. The nearby comment attributes this to row-level merging and leaves a TODO for vectorized reader support.
2. The FGR branch [passes that reader into SparkFileFormatInternalRowReaderContext](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/HoodieFileGroupReaderBasedFileFormat.scala#L304-L307).
3. [HoodieMergeOnReadRDDV2.scala, lines 113–125](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/hudi/HoodieMergeOnReadRDDV2.scala#L113-L125) also constructs its Parquet FGR base reader with `vectorized = false`, separately from `OPTION_RETURNING_BATCH = false`.
4. [Spark34ParquetReader.scala, lines 167–229](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark3.4.x/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/Spark34ParquetReader.scala#L167-L229) has distinct vectorized-decoding and row-based ParquetRecordReader branches. Its [builder](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/be8a54c4ebdaf287993d24fefba60a58952a9c9e/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark3.4.x/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/execution/datasources/parquet/Spark34ParquetReader.scala#L252-L295) passes the supplied `vectorized` argument into `enableVectorizedReader`; enabling Spark's vectorized-reader SQL setting alone does not override the explicit false in these FGR paths.

This concerns the reader supplied to FGR, not every MOR query or every base-file-only path. Likewise, `supportVectorizedRead: true` at the FileFormat level does not by itself demonstrate vectorized decoding inside FGR.

## Why investigate this?

For wide projections over base-plus-log file slices, column pruning eliminates little base-file work. Non-vectorized base decoding could therefore become a meaningful cost even if FGR improves other parts of the read path. This is a performance hypothesis, not evidence that the setting alone explains a cross-version regression. No isolated upstream before/after measurement is claimed here.

Vectorized decoding and returning ColumnarBatch to Spark are separate decisions. Could the base reader decode batches internally but expose compatible rows to the existing merge pipeline? This would not require vectorizing the merge algorithm itself. It is also not a proposal to simply flip the boolean without checking row representation, ownership and correctness.

## Proposed scope and validation

- Identify the constraints behind the current restriction: row representation (including UnsafeRow assumptions), batch-buffer reuse/lifetime, projection/schema evolution, and merge semantics.
- If feasible, support vectorized decoding for eligible Parquet base reads with row output, retaining a safe fallback for unsupported cases and covering both entry points above.
- Validate inserts, updates, partial updates, deletes, nulls, schema evolution and timestamp handling, including records retained across batch boundaries.
- Benchmark the current and candidate readers on the same upstream build baseline and frozen MOR snapshot, with identical resources and query expressions. Include narrow and full projections, base-plus-log slices, and base-only/log-only controls. Consume the projected values rather than relying on count(*) alone. Record scan/task time, input bytes, CPU/GC and spill, with repeated paired runs.

These are proposed validation steps, not completed results.

## Questions for maintainers

What correctness constraints must be addressed before vectorized base decoding can feed row-level FGR merging? In particular, which row-representation and buffer-lifetime contracts should an implementation preserve? If an existing implementation already covers this MOR-specific scope, please link it so this issue can be consolidated with that work.

### Task Type

Performance optimization

### Related Issues

- #17128 (HUDI-9674): umbrella Spark 1.X read-performance audit. It explicitly calls for exploring FGR vectorized reads; this issue proposes tracking that item separately.
- #20089 / PR #20090 and #20140 / PR #20193: related per-scan reader decisions and session-configuration mutation. Fixing those decisions is distinct from enabling vectorized decoding in the MOR-specific reader explicitly constructed with `false` at the pinned commit.
- #20182 / PR #20183: reports stale vectorization state and a `ColumnarBatchRow` / `UnsafeRow` mismatch, with a COW wide-nested-schema reproduction. Relevant to reader/output compatibility, but not evidence of the same failure in MOR merging.
- #17026 (HUDI-9443): reflection on `batchIdx` in the vectorized reader's per-row access. Relevant when considering a vectorized-decoding/row-output implementation; it does not itself address the MOR reader's explicit disablement.
- #20064: broader executor-overhead work in Hudi 1.x. Task serialization, configuration and schema work are separate performance factors, not attributed to vectorization by this issue.

### Bug Description

**What happened:**

Flink bucket pruning can silently omit existing rows when a compound record key contains the literal string `__empty__` or `__null__`.

For example, with record key fields `uuid,name`, eight buckets, and `(uuid='__empty__', name='x')`, the writer assigns the row to bucket **1**, but the reader's equality-filter pruning selects bucket **4**. An unfiltered scan returns the row, while filtering on both key fields returns no rows. This was reproduced with both COPY_ON_WRITE and MERGE_ON_READ tables.

**What you expected:**

An equality query on a stored compound key should return the same matching row as an unfiltered scan.

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Create a Flink Hudi table with a compound primary key and bucket index:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t1 (
  uuid STRING,
  name STRING,
  age INT,
  ts TIMESTAMP(3),
  `partition` STRING,
  PRIMARY KEY (uuid, name) NOT ENFORCED
) PARTITIONED BY (`partition`) WITH (
  'connector' = 'hudi',
  'path' = '/tmp/hudi-compound-key-bucket-pruning',
  'table.type' = 'COPY_ON_WRITE',
  'hoodie.datasource.write.recordkey.field' = 'uuid,name',
  'ordering.fields' = 'ts',
  'index.type' = 'BUCKET',
  'hoodie.bucket.index.num.buckets' = '8'
);

INSERT INTO t1 VALUES
  ('__empty__', 'x', 23, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:01', 'par1');
```

2. Run a batch scan and an equality query:

```sql
SELECT * FROM t1;
SELECT * FROM t1 WHERE name = 'x' AND uuid = '__empty__';
```

3. The first query returns the row, but the second returns an empty result. The same issue occurs with the literal `__null__` and with MERGE_ON_READ tables.

**Root cause:**

The writer hashes values extracted from the encoded record key using `KeyGenUtils.extractRecordKeysByFields`. For compound keys, that extraction maps `__empty__` to an empty string and `__null__` to null. `PrimaryKeyPruners.getBucketIdFunc` instead hashes the filter literals directly, producing a different bucket ID. The mismatch also applies when only a subset of the compound key fields is used for bucket hashing. Single-field keys retain the literal placeholder strings and must preserve that behavior.

### Environment

- Hudi: `1.3.0-SNAPSHOT`, reproduced against commit `a41f6eaf7df0`.
- Query engine: Flink 1.20.1, batch SQL.
- Java: 11.
- Table types: COPY_ON_WRITE and MERGE_ON_READ.
- Relevant configuration: compound record key `uuid,name`, bucket index, eight buckets.

### Logs and Stack Trace

This is a silent incorrect-result issue, not a query exception. Regression assertions against the unpatched implementation report:

```text
Bucket ID: expected: <1> but was: <4>
SQL result: expected: <[+I[__empty__, x, 23, 1970-01-01T00:00:01, par1]]> but was: <[]>
```

### What happened

Flink timestamp predicates can discard matching rows when a `TIMESTAMP(6)` literal is reduced to milliseconds before filtering.

For example, a Parquet row containing `1970-01-01T00:00:01.000001` is stored as `1000001` microseconds. An unfiltered read returns the correct timestamp, but the equality predicate is built as `eq(ts, 1000)`, causing the matching row group to be excluded. This Parquet filtering issue occurs independently of metadata/data-skipping indexes.

The same loss of precision affects other consumers of `ExpressionUtils.getValueFromLiteral()`:

- Column statistics and literals are both reduced to milliseconds. Values that differ within one millisecond become indistinguishable, so strict range comparisons and inequality can incorrectly exclude matching files.
- Record-index lookup reconstructs timestamp keys from milliseconds, losing the fractional component used by the writer when consistent logical timestamp keys are enabled.
- Timestamp bucket-pruning keys can differ from the writer's timestamp representation.

### Expected behavior

Preserve the full timestamp literal value. Convert to the required representation at the consumer boundary: milliseconds or microseconds for Parquet predicates, full-precision timestamps for statistics comparisons, and writer-compatible values for index keys.

### Reproduction

1. Write a Parquet file with an INT64 `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` column containing `1000001` (`1970-01-01T00:00:01.000001`).
2. Read it through Flink's Hudi `RecordIterators.getParquetRecordIterator()` using a `TIMESTAMP(6)` field without predicates. The row is returned correctly.
3. Repeat with an `ExpressionPredicates` equality predicate for the same timestamp. The original implementation returns no rows.

Additional focused reproductions:

- Set the timestamp column-statistics minimum and maximum to `1970-01-01T00:00:01.000002`, then evaluate `ts > TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:01.000001'`. The original evaluator incorrectly rejects the file.
- Derive a record-index lookup key for `1970-01-01T00:00:01.000001` with consistent logical timestamp keys enabled. The original lookup produces `1970-01-01T00:00:01`, while the writer produces `1970-01-01T00:00:01.000001`.

### Environment

### Description

Spark data skipping can silently omit matching rows after adding columns to the Column Stats Index (CSI).

After adding `name` to the indexed column list, existing files may still lack statistics for `name`, even though they contain non-null names. When a query references both an originally indexed column and the newly indexed column, the partially indexed file is incorrectly pruned.

For example, after changing the indexed column list from `age` to `age,name`:

- `name = 'alice'` returns the matching row.
- `age >= 0 AND name = 'alice'` incorrectly returns no rows with data skipping enabled.
- The same combined predicate returns the matching row with data skipping disabled.

This was reproduced with real Spark SQL writes and queries in a local regression test added to `TestDataSkippingQuery`.

### Environment

- Hudi: `master` at `a41f6eaf7df0`, `1.3.0-SNAPSHOT`.
- Spark: `3.5.9`.
- Scala: `2.12.18`.
- Java: `11`.
- Table type: `COPY_ON_WRITE`.
- Metadata and column statistics enabled.
- Partition statistics disabled to isolate file-level CSI pruning.

### Steps to reproduce

Use a fresh table location and wait for each INSERT to complete.

```sql
SET hoodie.metadata.enable=true;
SET hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.enable=true;
SET hoodie.metadata.index.partition.stats.enable=false;
SET hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.column.list=age;
SET hoodie.enable.data.skipping=false;

CREATE TABLE csi_partial_stats (
  id INT,
  name STRING,
  age INT,
  ts BIGINT,
  dt STRING
) USING hudi
TBLPROPERTIES (
  primaryKey = 'id',
  orderingFields = 'ts',
  type = 'cow'
)
PARTITIONED BY (dt)
LOCATION '/tmp/hudi-spark-csi-partial-stats';

-- The name column exists in the data, but only age is indexed.
INSERT INTO csi_partial_stats
VALUES (1, 'alice', 25, 1, 'par1');

SET hoodie.metadata.index.column.stats.column.list=age,name;

-- Writing to another partition leaves the old file untouched.
INSERT INTO csi_partial_stats
VALUES (2, 'bob', 30, 2, 'par2');

-- Returns (1, alice, 25).
SELECT id, name, age
FROM csi_partial_stats
WHERE age >= 0 AND name = 'alice';

SET hoodie.enable.data.skipping=true;

-- Explicitly update the table property: changing only the session setting
-- can leave the creation-time false setting in effect.
ALTER TABLE csi_partial_stats
SET TBLPROPERTIES ('hoodie.enable.data.skipping' = 'true');

REFRESH TABLE csi_partial_stats;

-- Returns (1, alice, 25).
SELECT id, name, age
FROM csi_partial_stats
WHERE name = 'alice';

-- Incorrectly returns no rows.
SELECT id, name, age
FROM csi_partial_stats
WHERE age >= 0 AND name = 'alice';
```

### Expected behavior

All three SELECTs should return:

```text
1, alice, 25
```

Enabling data skipping or adding a predicate satisfied by the matching row must not change the query result.

### Actual behavior

| Predicate | Data skipping | Actual result |
|---|---|---|
| `age >= 0 AND name = 'alice'` | Disabled | `(1, alice, 25)` |
| `name = 'alice'` | Enabled | `(1, alice, 25)` |
| `age >= 0 AND name = 'alice'` | Enabled | Empty |

The regression test confirms the required metadata state before executing these queries:

- The CSI definition includes both `age` and `name`.
- Two files have `age` statistics.
- Only one file has `name` statistics.
- Per-file statistics coverage is `{age}` for one file and `{age, name}` for the other.

The test fails at the final query assertion:

```text
Combined age/name predicate with data skipping enabled:
Expected Array([1,alice,25]), but got Array()
```

### Root cause

1. [`ColumnStatsIndexSupport`](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/a41f6eaf7df0/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/hudi/ColumnStatsIndexSupport.scala#L289-L313) pads missing per-file column statistics with `(null, null, null)`.

2. [`DataSkippingUtils.genColumnValuesEqualToExpression`](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/a41f6eaf7df0/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/hudi/DataSkippingUtils.scala#L495-L501) translates `name = 'alice'` into:

   ```sql
   name_minValue <= 'alice' AND name_maxValue >= 'alice'
   ```

   For the old file, both bounds are NULL, so this predicate evaluates to SQL NULL rather than conservatively retaining the file.

3. [`SparkBaseIndexSupport.getCandidateFiles`](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/a41f6eaf7df0/hudi-spark-datasource/hudi-spark-common/src/main/scala/org/apache/hudi/SparkBaseIndexSupport.scala#L115-L143) applies the translated predicate directly through `DataFrame.where`, which drops rows whose predicate evaluates to NULL. Its fallback only restores files entirely absent from the transposed index. The old file already appears because it has `age` statistics, so it is not restored.

For the name-only query, the old file is absent from the requested statistics projection and is retained by the unindexed-file fallback. Adding the `age` predicate causes the file to appear in that projection and exposes the incorrect pruning.

The data column is present from the first write; this is missing statistics, not a missing schema field or known all-null data.

### Suggested behavior

Treat unavailable column statistics as unknown and retain a file whenever the available statistics cannot prove that the predicate is unsatisfiable.

Spark already handles unknown null counts conservatively for `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`. Equality and range predicates also need to account for incomplete statistics without conflating them with known all-null columns.

### Validation

A local regression test was added to `TestDataSkippingQuery`:

```text
Data skipping retains files with missing column statistics after index expansion
```

The targeted ScalaTest run reproduced the incorrect empty result. Relevant sources were recompiled against locally built dependencies; a full Maven build and the complete test suite were not run. No production fix is included, and the regression test has not yet been published in a PR.

### Related issue

The Flink reader has a separately reproduced issue involving partial column-statistics coverage: [apache/hudi#20289](https://github.com/apache/hudi/issues/20289).

Its fallback only restores files entirely absent from the transposed index. The old file already appears because it has `age` statistics, so it is not restored.

For the name-only query, the old file is absent from the requested statistics projection and is retained by the unindexed-file fallback. Adding the `age` predicate causes the file to appear in that projection and exposes the incorrect pruning.

The data column is present from the first write; this is missing statistics, not a missing schema field or known all-null data.

### Suggested behavior

Treat unavailable column statistics as unknown and retain a file whenever the available statistics cannot prove that the predicate is unsatisfiable.

Spark already handles unknown null counts conservatively for `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`. Equality and range predicates also need to account for incomplete statistics without conflating them with known all-null columns.

### Validation

A local regression test was added to `TestDataSkippingQuery`:

```text
Data skipping retains files with missing column statistics after index expansion
```

The targeted ScalaTest run reproduced the incorrect empty result. Relevant sources were recompiled against locally built dependencies; a full Maven build and the complete test suite were not run. No production fix is included, and the regression test has not yet been published in a PR.

### Related issue

The Flink reader has a separately reproduced issue involving partial column-statistics coverage: [apache/hudi#20289](https://github.com/apache/hudi/issues/20289).

body_text:
### Bug Description

**What happened:**

On a Flink table with a bucket index, one primary key and two or more partition fields, an equality filter on the primary key returns no rows, while an unfiltered scan returns them. Such a table uses the complex key generator, whose default `FIELD_PREFIXED` encoding stores the record key as `uuid:id1`. The bucket writers hash that stored key through `KeyGenUtils.extractRecordKeysByFields`, which returns it unsplit because it only splits keys holding both `,` and `:`. `PrimaryKeyPruners.getBucketIdFunc` hashes the bare filter literal `id1` instead, so bucket pruning keeps another bucket's file group. With the default 4 buckets, every key of the reproducer below lands in a different bucket than the one the pruner picks, on both COPY_ON_WRITE and MERGE_ON_READ. Tables that store bare keys (`VALUE_ONLY`) are not affected.

**What you expected:**

`SELECT * FROM t1 WHERE uuid = 'id1'` returns the row that `SELECT * FROM t1` returns.

**Steps to reproduce:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE t1 (
  uuid VARCHAR(20),
  name VARCHAR(10),
  age INT,
  ts TIMESTAMP(3),
  `partition` VARCHAR(20),
  `region` VARCHAR(20),
  PRIMARY KEY (uuid) NOT ENFORCED
) PARTITIONED BY (`partition`, `region`) WITH (
  'connector' = 'hudi',
  'path' = '/tmp/hudi-bucket-pruning-prefixed-key',
  'index.type' = 'BUCKET'
);

INSERT INTO t1 VALUES
  ('id1', 'Danny', 23, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:01', 'par1', 'r1'),
  ('id2', 'Stephen', 33, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:02', 'par1', 'r2'),
  ('id3', 'Julian', 53, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:03', 'par2', 'r1'),
  ('id4', 'Fabian', 31, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:04', 'par2', 'r2'),
  ('id5', 'Sophia', 18, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:05', 'par3', 'r1'),
  ('id6', 'Emma', 20, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:06', 'par3', 'r2'),
  ('id7', 'Bob', 44, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:07', 'par4', 'r1'),
  ('id8', 'Han', 56, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:08', 'par4', 'r2');

SELECT * FROM t1;                    -- returns all 8 rows
SELECT * FROM t1 WHERE uuid = 'id1'; -- returns no rows
```

Reproducing test, added to `ITTestHoodieDataSource`:

```java
  @ParameterizedTest
  @MethodSource("tableTypeAndComplexKeyGenEncodingParams")
  void testBucketPruningWithSingleRecordKeyAndMultiplePartitionFields(HoodieTableType tableType, ComplexKeyGenEncoding encoding) {
    TableEnvironment tableEnv = batchTableEnv;
    // a single record key with two partition fields uses the complex key generator, which by default stores
    // the record key as `uuid:<value>` (FIELD_PREFIXED); legacy version 8 tables may store the bare value (VALUE_ONLY)
    String valueOnlyOptions = ",\n"
        + "  '" + HoodieTableConfig.COMPLEX_KEYGEN_ENCODING.key() + "' = '" + ComplexKeyGenEncoding.VALUE_ONLY + "',\n"
        + "  '" + FlinkOptions.WRITE_TABLE_VERSION.key() + "' = '" + HoodieTableVersion.EIGHT.versionCode() + "'";
    String hoodieTableDDL = "create table t1(\n"
        + "  uuid varchar(20),\n"
        + "  name varchar(10),\n"
        + "  age int,\n"
        + "  ts timestamp(3),\n"
        + "  `partition` varchar(20),\n"
        + "  `region` varchar(20),\n"
        + "  PRIMARY KEY(uuid) NOT ENFORCED\n"
        + ")\n"
        + "PARTITIONED BY (`partition`, `region`)\n"
        + "with (\n"
        + "  'connector' = 'hudi',\n"
        + "  'path' = '" + tempFile.getAbsolutePath() + "',\n"
        + "  '" + FlinkOptions.TABLE_TYPE.key() + "' = '" + tableType + "',\n"
        + "  '" + FlinkOptions.INDEX_TYPE.key() + "' = 'BUCKET'"
        + (encoding == ComplexKeyGenEncoding.VALUE_ONLY ? valueOnlyOptions : "")
        + "\n)";
    tableEnv.executeSql(hoodieTableDDL);

    execInsertSql(tableEnv, "insert into t1 values\n"
        + "('id1','Danny',23,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:01','par1','r1'),\n"
        + "('id2','Stephen',33,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:02','par1','r2'),\n"
        + "('id3','Julian',53,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:03','par2','r1'),\n"
        + "('id4','Fabian',31,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:04','par2','r2'),\n"
        + "('id5','Sophia',18,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:05','par3','r1'),\n"
        + "('id6','Emma',20,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:06','par3','r2'),\n"
        + "('id7','Bob',44,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:07','par4','r1'),\n"
        + "('id8','Han',56,TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:08','par4','r2')");
    assertEquals(encoding,
        HoodieTestUtils.createMetaClient(tempFile.getAbsolutePath()).getTableConfig().getComplexKeyGenEncoding().get());

    List<Row> allRows = CollectionUtil.iterableToList(
        () -> tableEnv.sqlQuery("select uuid from t1").execute().collect());
    assertEquals(8, allRows.size());
    // an equality filter on the record key must find the rows the unfiltered scan finds
    for (String uuid : Arrays.asList("id1", "id8")) {
      List<Row> result = CollectionUtil.iterableToList(
          () -> tableEnv.sqlQuery("select uuid from t1 where uuid = '" + uuid + "'").execute().collect());
      assertRowsEquals(result, "[+I[" + uuid + "]]");
    }
  }

  /**
   * Return test params => (HoodieTableType, ComplexKeyGenEncoding).
   */
  private static Stream<Arguments> tableTypeAndComplexKeyGenEncodingParams() {
    Object[][] data =
        new Object[][] {
            {HoodieTableType.COPY_ON_WRITE, ComplexKeyGenEncoding.FIELD_PREFIXED},
            {HoodieTableType.COPY_ON_WRITE, ComplexKeyGenEncoding.VALUE_ONLY},
            {HoodieTableType.MERGE_ON_READ, ComplexKeyGenEncoding.FIELD_PREFIXED},
            {HoodieTableType.MERGE_ON_READ, ComplexKeyGenEncoding.VALUE_ONLY}};
    return Stream.of(data).map(Arguments::of);
  }
```

In the live-coordinator branch of [`StreamWriteOperatorCoordinator.resetToCheckpoint()`](https://github.com/apache/hudi/blob/aabed46593960ff3553cdc1ace1a491987983702/hudi-flink-datasource/hudi-flink/src/main/java/org/apache/hudi/sink/StreamWriteOperatorCoordinator.java#L336-L351), **`restoreEvents(checkpointID)` should execute on the same event executor as normal event handling and checkpoint commits, using `executor.executeSync(...)`.** This orders recovery after previously accepted work and waits for recovery to finish before reset returns.

Currently, `resetToCheckpoint()` calls `restoreEvents()` directly on the JobManager main thread. During a global failover within the same execution graph, the coordinator instance and its executor survive. Canceling the old tasks does not drain this executor, so recovery can overlap an ongoing commit.

For example:

1. The executor is processing `notifyCheckpointComplete(K)` and committing instant `T`. The commit has not completed, and its event buffer is still present.
2. A global failover occurs, and Flink calls `resetToCheckpoint(K)` on the same coordinator.
3. `restoreEvents(K)` runs outside the executor, sees that `T` is not completed, and starts another commit for `T` while the original invocation is still in progress.
4. Both commit calls can succeed, producing two physical completed timeline files with different completion times and invoking an enabled commit callback twice.

A deterministic coordinator-level test with real timeline writes reproduced both effects on Hudi `1.3.0-SNAPSHOT` (`aabed465939`), Flink `1.20.1`, and timeline layout v2.

Running recovery synchronously through the executor lets the earlier commit finish and remove its event buffer before `restoreEvents()` checks what remains to be committed.

body_text:
### Task Description

**What needs to be done:**

On each discovery pass, the Flink streaming reader (`IncrementalInputSplits` → `WriteProfiles.getFilesFromMetadata`) checks that every file written by the new commits still exists, because the cleaner may have removed some. It makes one `StreamerUtil.fileExists` call per file, serially, on the JobManager's split enumerator thread.

Proposal: on a high level, group files by partitions, like group all files under 2026/10/14, and then do a single LIST call to this partition to get all files under this partition. This avoids having to issue 1 request per file.

More details:
- Group candidate files by parent directory. When two or more candidates share a directory, list it once and check membership against the listing. Directories with a single candidate keep a single `exists` call.
- Process directories in parallel with a bounded pool, set by a new option such as `read.file-existence-check.parallelism` (default 8).
- Keep the reverse-commit-order resolution, so a file touched by several commits resolves to its latest surviving version.

Alternatives considered:
- **Parallel per-file `exists` with a large pool (for example 100 threads).** Wall time is similar (~36 s estimated for the table below), but it still sends one request per file. That's ~197K requests per pass, about 5.5K/s at 100 threads, which risks object-store throttling and it is capped by filesystem connection-pool limits. Grouping by directory sends ~49× fewer requests with a small pool.
- **Answering existence from the metadata table's `files` partition.** No storage calls at all, but it only works for tables with the metadata table enabled. The listing approach works for every table.

**Why this task is needed:**
On large COW tables with scattered upserts, almost every file group is rewritten by every commit, so each discovery pass checks one file per file group.

Production example: a COW table with ~10B rows (~28 TB) on GCS, partitioned by date into ~4,000 partitions, with ~197K file groups. Each commit rewrites ~197K files.

| | Before | After (prototype) |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate files per pass | 197,191 | 197,191 |
| Storage calls | ~197K `exists`, serial | 4,027 directory listings, 8 in parallel |
| Latency per call | ~18 ms average | p50 85 ms / p90 132 ms / p99 245 ms |
| Existence check | ~3,600 s | 51.4 s |
| Total discovery pass | ~60 min | 56.5 s (~64× faster) |

In the prototype, the existence check is now 51 s of the 56.5 s pass. The rest is timeline analysis 2.5 s, commit metadata 0.9 s, collecting candidates 1.4 s, and building splits 1.0 s.

Slow discovery also causes duplicate splits. Flink's `ExecutorNotifier` schedules discovery at a fixed rate, so a pass that takes longer than `read.streaming.check-interval` (300 s here) is followed immediately by another. That next pass starts from a position that hasn't advanced yet and rediscovers the same commits. Keeping discovery well under the interval avoids this.

## Describe the problem you faced

`HoodieIndexer` cannot rebuild a **partitioned** record-level index. When it re-enables indexes for metadata partitions that already exist on storage, it maps the on-storage partition name `record_index` to `hoodie.metadata.global.record.level.index.enable` unconditionally, with no branch for the partitioned variant.

Since the write happens *after* the user's `--props` are loaded, an explicitly supplied `hoodie.metadata.record.level.index.enable=true` is overwritten. There is no workaround via configuration.

`hudi-utilities/src/main/java/org/apache/hudi/utilities/HoodieIndexer.java:180-190`:

```java
Set<String> initializedMetadataPartitions = getInflightAndCompletedMetadataPartitions(metaClient.getTableConfig());
initializedMetadataPartitions.forEach(p -> {
  ...
  if (PARTITION_NAME_RECORD_INDEX.equals(p)) {
    props.setProperty(GLOBAL_RECORD_LEVEL_INDEX_ENABLE_PROP.key(), "true");   // always global
  }
});
```

`RECORD_LEVEL_INDEX_ENABLE_PROP` (`hoodie.metadata.record.level.index.enable`) is not imported or referenced anywhere in the class. Both configs are declared adjacently in `HoodieMetadataConfig` (lines 362 and 370), and both index variants share the same `record_index` partition name (`HoodieTableMetadataUtil.PARTITION_NAME_RECORD_INDEX`), so the partition name alone cannot distinguish them.

## To Reproduce

1. Create a table with a partitioned record-level index (`hoodie.metadata.record.level.index.enable=true`).
2. Run `HoodieIndexer` against it in any mode that reaches `start()`, passing the same key in `--props`.
3. The index is rebuilt as a **global** record-level index, with default file-group sizing rather than the partitioned layout's.

## Expected behavior

The indexer should rebuild the index in the same shape it found. Distinguishing the two likely needs the table config or the existing index definition rather than the partition name — for example reading `hoodie.table.metadata.partitions` alongside whichever enable flag the table was built with, and setting the matching property.

## Environment Description

* Hudi version : 1.2.0 and master (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT)
* Running on Docker? : no

## Additional context

Introduced in 80381808a6c3 ("fix: Fixing record index related configs and enums", #14180, 2025-11-05), which split the record-index enable flag into global and partitioned variants. The indexer was updated to the global constant only. Shipped in 1.2.0.

Found while reviewing apache/hudi#20153, which adds a record-index sizing health check. That check's remedy suggests re-running `HoodieIndexer` to resize an undersized index; on a partitioned index that advice cannot currently work, so the remedy text there is being adjusted to say so until this is fixed.

body_text:
### Bug Description

**What happened:**

On a MERGE_ON_READ table at table version 8 or 9, Spark log compaction fails when the file slice it compacts holds a delete block and the ordering field is a string or a decimal. The error is `java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Unsupported type of the value (class org.apache.hudi.Spark3HoodieUTF8String)`, or `(class org.apache.spark.sql.types.Decimal)` for a decimal ordering field.

Log compaction reads the file slice with the file group reader. That reader converts the ordering value of every delete-block entry to the Spark engine type, so it can be compared with the data records (`BufferedRecords.fromDeleteRecord` -> `RecordContext.getOrderingValue(DeleteRecord)`): a string becomes a `HoodieUTF8String` and a decimal becomes a Spark `Decimal`. `FileGroupReaderBasedInlineLogAppendHandle` writes these deletes back as `HoodieEmptyRecord`s that keep the engine value, but `HoodieDeleteBlock` can only serialize Java types.

Since #19283, log compaction of a data table reads through the Spark reader context, so the default Avro record merger is affected as well as the Spark one. With `hoodie.log.compaction.inline=true`, the failure surfaces in the write that triggers log compaction (`BaseHoodieTableServiceClient.inlineLogCompact`).

**What you expected:**

Log compaction writes the deletes back with the Java ordering values they had in the delete block. Later reads should still order the deletes correctly against older and newer updates.

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Create a MERGE_ON_READ table at table version 9 with a string ordering field `ts`, `EVENT_TIME_ORDERING` and `hoodie.log.compaction.enable=true`.
2. Insert `id1` and `id2`.
3. Delete `id1` with `_hoodie_is_deleted=true`, which writes a delete block.
4. Update `id2`, which writes a data block in the same file slice.
5. Run log compaction, either with `SparkRDDWriteClient.scheduleLogCompaction` and `logCompact` or through `hoodie.log.compaction.inline=true` on a later write.

The reproducing test in `TestMORDataSource` fails on master for every row:

```scala
  @ParameterizedTest
  @CsvSource(value = Array("AVRO;string;8", "AVRO;decimal(10,2);9", "SPARK;string;9", "SPARK;decimal(10,2);8"), delimiter = ';')
  def testLogCompactionRewritesDeletesWithEngineOrdering(recordType: HoodieRecordType, orderingType: String, tableVersion: Int): Unit = {
    val (writeOpts, readOpts) = getWriterReaderOpts(recordType)
    val opts = writeOpts ++ Map(
      TABLE_TYPE.key -> MOR_TABLE_TYPE_OPT_VAL,
      RECORDKEY_FIELD.key -> "id",
      PARTITIONPATH_FIELD.key -> "",
      HoodieTableConfig.ORDERING_FIELDS.key -> "ts",
      HoodieWriteConfig.RECORD_MERGE_MODE.key -> RecordMergeMode.EVENT_TIME_ORDERING.name(),
      HoodieWriteConfig.WRITE_TABLE_VERSION.key -> tableVersion.toString,
      HoodieTableConfig.VERSION.key -> tableVersion.toString,
      HoodieCompactionConfig.INLINE_COMPACT.key -> "false",
      HoodieCompactionConfig.ENABLE_LOG_COMPACTION.key -> "true",
      HoodieCompactionConfig.LOG_COMPACTION_BLOCKS_THRESHOLD.key -> "1")

    def write(rows: Seq[(String, String, Boolean)], mode: SaveMode): Unit = {
      val localSpark = spark
      import localSpark.implicits._
      rows.toDF("id", "ts", "_hoodie_is_deleted")
        .withColumn("ts", col("ts").cast(orderingType))
        .coalesce(1).write.format("hudi").options(opts).mode(mode).save(basePath)
    }

    write(Seq(("id1", "100", false), ("id2", "100", false)), SaveMode.Overwrite)
    // The delete lands in a delete block, the update in a data block of the same file slice.
    write(Seq(("id1", "110", true)), SaveMode.Append)
    write(Seq(("id2", "120", false)), SaveMode.Append)

    val client = DataSourceUtils.createHoodieClient(spark.sparkContext, "", basePath, tableName, opts.asJava)
      .asInstanceOf[SparkRDDWriteClient[HoodieRecordPayload[Nothing]]]
    try {
      val logCompactionInstant = client.scheduleLogCompaction(Option.empty()).get()
      client.logCompact(logCompactionInstant, true)
    } finally {
      client.close()
    }

    def readOrdering(): Map[String, Int] = spark.read.format("hudi").options(readOpts).load(basePath)
      .select("id", "ts").collect().map(row => row.getString(0) -> BigDecimal(row.get(1).toString).toInt).toMap

    // The compacted delete keeps its ordering value: an older update leaves id1 deleted, a newer one brings it back.
    write(Seq(("id1", "105", false)), SaveMode.Append)
    assertEquals(Map("id2" -> 120), readOrdering())
    write(Seq(("id1", "115", false)), SaveMode.Append)
    assertEquals(Map("id1" -> 115, "id2" -> 120), readOrdering())
  }
```

### Environment

**Hudi version:** master since #19283, with `hoodie.write.table.version` 8 or 9. 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 log-compact through `HoodieAvroReaderContext` and do not hit this failure.
**Query engine:** Spark
**Relevant configs:** `hoodie.log.compaction.enable=true` or `hoodie.log.compaction.inline=true`, a string or decimal ordering field, table version 8 or 9

### Logs and Stack Trace

Log compaction in the reproducing test on master:

```
org.apache.hudi.exception.HoodieAppendException: Failed while appending records to <table>/.<fileId>-0_<instant>.log.1_0-79-148
	at org.apache.hudi.io.HoodieInlineLogAppendHandle.appendDataAndDeleteBlocks(HoodieInlineLogAppendHandle.java:243)
	at org.apache.hudi.io.HoodieInlineLogAppendHandle.flushAppend(HoodieInlineLogAppendHandle.java:163)
	at org.apache.hudi.io.HoodieAppendHandle.doAppend(HoodieAppendHandle.java:161)
	at org.apache.hudi.io.FileGroupReaderBasedInlineLogAppendHandle.doAppend(FileGroupReaderBasedInlineLogAppendHandle.java:112)
	at org.apache.hudi.table.action.compact.HoodieCompactor.logCompact(HoodieCompactor.java:185)
	...
Caused by: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Unsupported type of the value (class org.apache.hudi.Spark3HoodieUTF8String)
	at org.apache.hudi.common.avro.HoodieAvroWrapperUtils.wrapValueIntoAvro(HoodieAvroWrapperUtils.java:159)
	at org.apache.hudi.common.table.log.block.HoodieDeleteBlock.lambda$serializeV3$2(HoodieDeleteBlock.java:162)
	...
	at org.apache.hudi.common.table.log.block.HoodieDeleteBlock.serializeV3(HoodieDeleteBlock.java:164)
	at org.apache.hudi.common.table.log.block.HoodieDeleteBlock.getContentBytes(HoodieDeleteBlock.java:109)
	at org.apache.hudi.common.table.log.HoodieLogFormatWriter.appendBlocks(HoodieLogFormatWriter.java:147)
	at org.apache.hudi.io.HoodieInlineLogAppendHandle.appendDataAndDeleteBlocks(HoodieInlineLogAppendHandle.java:230)
```

The decimal rows fail the same way with `Unsupported type of the value (class org.apache.spark.sql.types.Decimal)`.
